title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline.
abstract:
Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function.
We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models.
In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively).
Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

title: Integration of blood-based biomarkers and genomic variants identifies individuals with mild cognitive impairment who benefit from multidomain intervention.
abstract:
Our recent Japan-Multimodal Intervention Trial for the Prevention of Dementia (J-MINT) trial suggested that multidomain lifestyle interventions may delay cognitive decline. However, substantial interindividual variability in response persists, and identifying individuals more likely to benefit from the intervention remains challenging. Blood-based biomarkers (BBMs), which provide a minimally invasive means of assessing Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathological processes, may help identify biologically distinct subgroups of individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
Blood-based biomarkers-including amyloid-β42/40 ratio, phosphorylated tau-217, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-were measured in J-MINT participants. Hierarchical clustering based on BBM profiles was used to identify biologically defined subgroups. Whole-genome sequencing data were analyzed using genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) to identify genetic variants associated with the BBM-based subgroup. A prediction model for the subgroup assignment was constructed using the associated incorporating the genetic variants, age, sex, and apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) allele count. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation repeated 1000 times.
BBM-based clustering identified a subgroup characterized by elevated GFAP and multiple biomarker abnormalities. Within this subgroup, the change in cognitive performance from baseline to 18 months differed significantly between intervention and control groups, with greater decline observed in the control group. GWAS identified four variants showing suggestive association with the subgroup, two of which were located in intronic regions of genes associated with hearing loss (PCDH15 and ATP11A).
BBM-based clustering identified biologically distinct subgroups among individuals with MCI. The subgroup characterized by multiple biomarker abnormalities and elevated GFAP showed differential cognitive trajectories between the intervention and control groups. These findings suggest that BBMs, potentially in combination with genetic information, may help identify individuals with a more progressive AD-related biological profile who may derive greater benefit from multidomain intervention.

title: Depression and amyloid-β across CSF, PET, and plasma biomarkers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease is increasingly defined by biomarker evidence of amyloid-β and tau pathology, sharpening questions about whether late-life depression contributes to, or instead reflects, this pathology. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published between 2000 and 2025 that compared amyloid-β biomarkers in adults with and without depression, with depression defined by validated clinical diagnoses or symptom rating scales. Twenty-four studies were included, spanning three biomarker sources: cerebrospinal fluid, positron emission tomography imaging, and plasma. Across all sources, the pooled difference in amyloid-β burden between depressed and non-depressed individuals was small and clustered near zero, indicating only a weak, statistically non-significant tendency toward higher amyloid in depression. When the three sources were examined separately, each yielded a similar near-null result, although between-study heterogeneity was considerable for cerebrospinal fluid and plasma and moderate for imaging. Importantly, a prespecified subgroup analysis showed that imaging results diverged by quantification method: studies using the simpler standardized uptake value ratio clustered around zero, whereas the smaller group of studies using kinetic distribution volume ratio modelling showed a significant positive association, suggesting that methodological choices critically influence the observed relationship. Taken together, these findings indicate that depression is not consistently accompanied by greater amyloid-β burden across widely used biomarker platforms. The distribution volume ratio signal nonetheless raises the possibility of subtle associations that cruder methods may obscure, and suggests that depression may shape Alzheimer's disease trajectories more by modifying the clinical impact of amyloid than by altering its amount.

title: Affective symptoms in focal epilepsy: A scoping review of localization and lateralizing findings.
abstract: Emotional experiences during focal seizures are often misinterpreted as psychiatric disorders. We aimed to evaluate symptoms involving affective symptoms at seizure onset. We aimed to identify the most prevalent affective symptoms at seizure onset and characterize their localizing and lateralizing value. We performed a scoping review based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses-extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. A systematic search identified records from 4 databases: PubMed, Embase, CINAHL (via EBSCOhost), and Web of Science. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. This review focused on patients with focal seizures, as affective symptoms may occur in generalized epilepsies. The affective symptoms: fear, anxiety, panic, sadness, mystic, ecstatic, sexual, and mirth were identified, and semiology was evaluated in accordance with ILAE guidelines. Symptom onset, frequency, brain localization, and video-EEG monitoring technique were evaluated to assess localization and lateralization of regional networks. Scalp EEG, invasive EEG recordings, and electrical stimulation were analyzed. A total of 1276 documents were identified, with 98 studies included for review. Fear was the most frequently reported ictal emotion, identified in 274 patients (66%), predominantly in temporal lobe epilepsy. Sadness and sexual, ecstatic symptoms were also consistently associated with temporal networks. Mirth was more frequently reported with frontal onset seizures. Evidence, primarily from Class IV studies, reported right hemispheric predominance for ecstasy, mystic, and sexual symptoms at seizure onset. Ictal affective symptoms at seizure onset yield localizing information. The limbic system, especially the temporal lobe, followed by the frontal lobe, was the most common site of origin. Fear was the most common spontaneous and electrically elicited symptom, followed by anxiety. While bi-hemispheric lateralization occurred, right lateralization predominated. Recognizing paroxysmal affective symptoms as ictal phenomena may reduce misdiagnosis and aid presurgical evaluation in drug-resistant focal epilepsy.

title: Associations of Antibodies Against Several Infections With Alzheimer Disease Neuropathology: A Prospective Cohort Study Analysis.
abstract:
Associations of common infections with Alzheimer disease (AD) risk have been reported. A hypothesized mechanism for these is cerebral β-amyloid (Aβ) aggregation as a defense to infection. We studied whether serologic measures of several infections in the UK population are associated with measures of AD neuropathology.
This prospective association study used data from the 1946 British birth cohort. Circulating antibodies against 14 pathogens, measured at age 60-64 years, were modelled as pathogen serostatus (indicating lifetime exposure to an agent), pathogen burden indices (measuring cumulative exposure to 2+ pathogens), and seroreactivity tertiles (indicating recent immunologic activity against pathogens). Associations of these were tested with plasma phosphorylated tau at threonine 217 (p-tau217) (primary outcome) and Aβ status (secondary outcome), measured with PET scans, at ages 69-71 years. Modelling used multivariable quantile and logistic regression. Model 1 adjusted for sex and ages at serology and outcome assessment, and models 2 and 3 additionally adjusted for APOE ε4 carriage and education, respectively. We also tested for interactions in associations by APOE ε4 carriage, education, and sex, and for interactions between herpes simplex virus 1 exposure with cytomegalovirus (CMV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV) exposure.
A total of 1,356 and 424 individuals had complete data for p-tau217 and Aβ-PET analyses, respectively. Mean age at p-tau217 was 69.9 years (SD 0.7), and 51.3% of participants were female. Median p-tau217 was 0.30 pg/mL (interquartile range 0.21-0.44). 28.3% had Aβ-positive scans. No notable associations were observed for serology measures with either outcome in main models, except for an unexpected association of herpes simplex virus 2 seropositivity with lower p-tau217 at the 75th quantile (-0.07 pg/mL in seropositive individuals; 95% CI -0.10 to -0.03). Odds of Aβ-PET positivity may have been higher for individuals seropositive for Epstein-Barr virus (odds ratio [OR] 2.84; 95% CI 0.95-8.52) and Toxoplasma gondii (OR 1.69; 95% CI 0.94-3.05). There were also potential interactions in p-tau217 associations by APOE ε4 carriage (for Helicobacter pylori and CMV) and educational attainment (for H pylori).
These findings do not imply associations between exposures to many common infections and AD neuropathologies. The possibility of pathogen interactions with APOE ε4 carriage and education in relation to AD neuropathology warrants further study.

title: Evidence for Reduced Somatic T-Cell Receptor Sequence Diversity Profiles Among Midwestern Amish in an Aging Cohort Study.
abstract:
The causes of late onset Alzheimer disease (LOAD) are not known but several recent lines of evidence implicate the adaptive immune system.
To characterize the adaptive immune system among Midwestern Amish participating in longitudinal studies of aging.
We immunosequenced the T-cell receptor (TCR) beta chain from genomic DNA of 72 participants, including those with clinically diagnosed LOAD (n = 6), mild cognitive impairment (MCI; n = 16), cognitive impairment but not AD (n = 3), and 35 cognitively unaffected. For a subset of participants, LOAD pathogenesis plasma biomarkers were available.
TCR sequence diversity measured as Simpson's clonality was lower among LOAD+MCI compared with non-LOAD, but these differences were not independent of age. Relatively few clonotypes (exact nucleotide sequences) were shared across participants; of those few shared include the Epstein Barr virus associated clonotype. HLA-A*03:01 and several HLA-DRB1 alleles were under-represented among LOAD+MCI participants compared with cognitively unaffected participants, but these associations were no longer significant in adjusted analyses. Among LOAD+MCI participants, increased p-tau181 was nominally associated with decreased TCR sequence diversity, and the nominal association was independent of age; however, this association did not remain statistically significant after strict correction for multiple testing and the limited sample size precluded formal tests of heterogeneity.
In this limited Midwestern Amish sample, the preliminary TCR diversity trends are consistent with the involvement of the adaptive immune system in LOAD.

title: Baseline MRI markers and clinical outcomes during anti-amyloid β therapy: A real-world study in a Japanese dementia center.
abstract:
Predictors of decline and of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) during anti-amyloid β therapy in routine care are undefined.
To identify baseline predictors of cognitive, functional, and safety outcomes.
Retrospective cohort of 161 consecutive patients initiating anti-amyloid β therapy at a Tokyo dementia center, 2024 to 2026 (lecanemab, 89; donanemab, 72).
Lecanemab or donanemab.
Change in MMSE and CDR-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB); baseline medial temporal atrophy (VSRAD Z score), amyloid PET burden, and microbleeds; ARIA.
With lecanemab, MMSE and CDR-SB declined significantly at every assessment (CDR-SB +0.79, +1.10, +1.60 at 6, 12, 18 months); memory and orientation declined while language was preserved. Greater baseline medial temporal atrophy was associated with greater 12-month CDR-SB worsening (r = 0.39; P = .01; n = 40); patients in the most severe standard category (Z ≥ 3) worsened by 2.62 versus 0.64 points (adjusted β = +2.18; P < .001). Atrophy was associated with older age (r = 0.19; P = .03) and with baseline memory-related measures - ADAS-Cog score (r = 0.32; P < .001) and the MMSE subdomains of delayed recall (β = -0.25; P = .006) and time orientation (β = -0.30; P = .04) - but not MMSE total score. Amyloid PET burden showed no significant association at most time points. All ARIA events were asymptomatic; ARIA-H occurred in 6 of 25 with microbleeds versus 3 of 136 without (odds ratio, 14.0; P < .001). Donanemab follow-up was 6 months.
Baseline medial temporal atrophy was associated with functional decline and microbleeds with ARIA-H. Pretreatment MRI may provide prognostic and safety information during anti-amyloid β therapy.

title: Association between IGFBP-3 and longitudinal neuropsychiatric symptom trajectories in early Parkinson's disease: a longitudinal cohort study.
abstract:
Neuropsychiatric symptoms are common in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet biomarkers associated with their long-term progression remain poorly characterized. Insulin-like growth factor binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) is involved in neurotrophic and metabolic processes. We examined whether baseline IGFBP-3 was associated with subsequent anxiety and depressive symptom trajectories in patients with early PD.
This longitudinal cohort included 352 patients with early-stage PD followed annually for up to 7 years. Anxiety and depressive symptoms were assessed using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) and 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), respectively. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated IGFBP-3 × time interactions, with adjustment for demographic, disease-related, metabolic, systemic, and treatment-related covariates, including time-varying levodopa-equivalent daily dose.
In fully adjusted longitudinal models, each 1-SD higher baseline IGFBP-3 was associated with a slower annual increase in STAI (β=-0.41 points/year; 95% CI, - 0.60 to - 0.22; P < 0.001) and GDS scores (β=-0.055 points/year; 95% CI, - 0.082 to - 0.028; P < 0.001). By Year 7, adjusted STAI scores were 68.5 in the low and 63.4 in the high IGFBP-3 tertile, corresponding to a difference of 5.1 points (95% CI, 2.8-7.4; P < 0.001); corresponding GDS scores were 3.17 and 2.36. After mutual adjustment, the IGFBP-3 × time association remained evident for STAI (β=-0.36; 95% CI, - 0.57 to - 0.15; P = 0.001) and GDS (β=-0.049; 95% CI, - 0.079 to - 0.019; P = 0.002). The molar IGF-1/IGFBP-3 ratio was not associated with longitudinal changes in STAI (P = 0.433) or GDS (P = 0.498).
Higher baseline IGFBP-3 was associated with slower progression of anxiety and depressive symptoms over 7 years in early PD, suggesting that IGFBP-3 may capture clinically relevant information on neuropsychiatric symptom progression.

title: Brexpiprazole for Individual Agitation Symptoms in Alzheimer's Dementia: A Caregiver-Centered Post Hoc Analysis.
abstract:
People with Alzheimer's dementia commonly experience agitation symptoms, which are distressing to caregivers and can influence long-term care decisions. The aim of this exploratory post hoc analysis was to test the hypothesis that brexpiprazole can improve individual agitation symptoms over 12 and 24 weeks, including symptoms that caregivers find the most distressing.
Data were included from two phase 3, 12-week, randomized (brexpiprazole or placebo), double-blind trials and a phase 3, 12-week, brexpiprazole-treatment extension trial. Participants had Alzheimer's dementia with agitation, and lived at home or in long-term care. The frequency of 29 agitation symptoms over 12 and 24 weeks was assessed using Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory (CMAI) item scores. The focus of this post hoc analysis was the 11 CMAI agitation symptoms that caregivers found the most distressing in a prior survey.
Among 610 participants (median age 74 years, 55.5% female, 44.5% male), each of the 11 most-distressing agitation symptoms reduced in frequency from baseline to Week 12, with further improvements to Week 24 (n = 159). Improvements over 12 weeks were numerically greater with brexpiprazole 2 or 3 mg/day (n = 363) compared with placebo (n = 247) on 9 of 11 symptoms: cursing or verbal aggression, spitting, repetitive sentences or questions, hitting, constant unwarranted requests for attention/help, trying to get to a different place, pacing or aimless wandering, grabbing onto people or things, and kicking. Each of the 18 other agitation symptoms (beyond the most distressing) also reduced in frequency. After 24 weeks, 15 of 29 agitation symptoms occurred less than once a week.
Brexpiprazole was associated with improvement in a range of agitation symptoms in people with Alzheimer's dementia, including those that are the most distressing to caregivers. These exploratory results suggest that brexpiprazole may improve the specific agitation symptoms that can have the biggest impact on the caregiver experience.

title: Terminal agitation in dementia: Challenges and opportunities.
abstract: Terminal agitation (TA), also referred to as terminal restlessness or terminal delirium, is a complex, multifactorial clinical syndrome that occurs at the end of life. While TA is evident in dementia (including Alzheimer's disease), it is not exclusive to the condition and also occurs in other terminal illnesses, e.g., cancer. Currently, no clinical tools exist or have been validated to assess TA in dementia. This may hinder the correct identification of TA and further contribute to the incorrect estimation of TA prevalence. Due to the complex diagnostic profile of TA, it may be frequently underrecognized in individuals with dementia. There is also a lack of consensus on clinical terminology, operational definition (e.g., temporality, symptomology) and conceptualization of TA. This may be attributed in part to cultural context and the variability in describing the final stages of dementia. Thus, reported prevalence rates of TA in dementia are heterogeneous in the literature. Further, using multiple descriptions or terms for TA in the literature suggests that the syndrome may occur in groups, or clusters of symptoms. There is an association between pain, agitation, and delirium in various stages of dementia, particularly at the end of life. Differentiating TA, or delirium from behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) is often difficult. The complex interaction between TA, dementia, and overlapping BPSD remains poorly understood and underresearched. Therefore, we outline priorities for future action and research, including the development of diagnostic and assessment tools to identify TA in dementia, and the establishment of consistent criteria for defining this syndrome.

title: Lifestyle, APOE ε4, amyloid burden, and race/ethnicity differences in cognition, mood, and anxiety among cognitively unimpaired older adults.
abstract:
We assessed whether lifestyle, race/ethnicity, and apolipoprotein E gene (APOE) ε4 were associated with cognition or mood/anxiety.
This secondary cohort analysis used data from the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) Study and the Longitudinal Evaluation of Amyloid Risk and Neurodegeneration (LEARN) cohort. Cognitively unimpaired adults aged 65 to 85 years (n = 1705) reported baseline lifestyle behaviors (summed as healthy lifestyle index [HLI]). APOE ε4 carrier status and amyloid positron emission tomography were assessed at baseline, while cognitive, anxiety, and depressive outcomes were assessed longitudinally. Associations were tested using mixed-effects models.
Among Non-Hispanic White participants, higher HLI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms, sufficient sleep was associated with smaller ε4-related increases in anxiety, and excessive alcohol use amplified ε4-related cognitive decline. Among participants from other racial/ethnic groups, walking and higher HLI were associated with more favorable anxiety/depression trajectories.
Adequate sleep, limited alcohol, walking, and no smoking may support emotional and cognitive health.

title: Beyond seizure control: Non-seizure-related outcomes in focal-onset epilepsy treated with adjunctive cenobamate. Third interim results from the BLESS study.
abstract:
Cenobamate is approved for treatment of focal seizures in adults, but evidence on non-seizure outcomes remains limited. This interim statistical analysis of the cenoBamate in aduLts with focal-onsEt SeizureS (BLESS) study evaluated patient- and clinician-reported outcomes for up to 52 weeks of cenobamate treatment.
BLESS is an observational, retrospective and prospective cohort study designed to assess the real-world effectiveness and safety of adjunctive cenobamate in adults with uncontrolled focal epilepsy. Outcomes included patient-reported health-related quality of life, sleepiness, anxiety, mood, and global functioning assessed by the 31-item Quality of Life in Epilepsy Inventory (QOLIE-31), the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and the Clinical Global Impression (CGI) scales.
A total of 377 participants were included. Among subjects with an available score at 12 (n = 197), 24 (n = 363), and 52 (n = 197) weeks, the QOLIE-31 overall score remained stable. Subjects with sustained seizure freedom at 24 weeks showed a significantly higher QOLIE-31 overall score (p = 0.041) and cognitive functioning scores (p = 0.019) compared with those who did not reach sustained seizure freedom. More than 68% of participants had normal daytime sleepiness (total ESS score 0-10) and did not report anxiety or depression according to the HADS-A and HADS-D subscales at each assessment up to 52 weeks. Clinicians rated 91.3% (n/N = 179/196), 85.7% (n/N = 300/350), and 87.4% (n/N = 167/191) of subjects as improved for their overall condition from the initiation of treatment according to the CGI-Improvement or change (CGI-I) scale, at 12, 24, and 52 weeks.
This interim analysis provides preliminary descriptive evidence on non-seizure outcomes in subjects treated with adjunctive cenobamate. Patient-reported outcome scores remained stable from 12 weeks and up to 52 weeks, consistent with preserved overall well-being. Better quality of life and cognitive functioning emerged in sustained vs non-sustained seizure-free participants. Based on clinicians' judgment, there was signal of improvement in overall condition compared to baseline in most treated subjects throughout the observation period.

title: TGF-β Inhibition Attenuates Tau Accumulation and Neurodegeneration in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Patient-Derived Organoids.
abstract:
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a devastating 4-repeat tauopathy with no approved disease-modifying treatments. Recent evidence showed increased transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) levels in PSP patient-derived ventral midbrain organoids (vMOs) and serum neuronally derived exosomes.
This study investigated whether TGF-β pharmacological inhibition could mitigate PSP pathology in vMOs.
Ninety-six vMOs were generated from induced pluripotent stem cells from two PSP-Richardson's syndrome patients and two healthy control donors (HCs). From day 60 to day 90, PSP organoids were (1) exposed to TGF-β receptor I inhibitor (SB431542); (2) exposed to recombinant TGF-β1, TGF-β2, and TGF-β3; or (3) untreated. At day 90, several tau species were assessed by immunoblotting; neurodegeneration was evaluated through TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH], neurofilament light chain [NfL]); astrocytic activation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) marker was evaluated by immunofluorescence, and histopathological hallmarks were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. An HC-derived organoid subgroup was exposed to the treatment conditions to assess potential toxicity.
At day 90, untreated PSP-derived vMOs exhibited increased phosphorylated tau levels (Ser396, Thr181, Ser202/Ser205 [AT8]) compared with HC-derived vMOs, dopaminergic neuron loss (reduced TH, increased NfL), and astrocytic reactivity (increased GFAP), along with PSP characteristic tau deposition. Tau hyperphosphorylation, neurodegeneration, and astrocytic reactivity were all markedly reduced in PSP-derived vMOs treated with TGF-β receptor I inhibitor. Conversely, exposure to TGF-β exacerbated these features. No toxic effects were observed in HC vMOs exposed to treatment conditions.
Pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling prevented key PSP molecular alterations in patient-derived organoids. These findings support further research and pave the way for future investigation of TGF-β-targeting strategies in clinical trials in patients with PSP. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Recent advances in the management of Lewy body dementia: evaluating progress and future directions.
abstract:
Lewy body dementia (LBD), encompassing dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD), is progressive and heterogeneous in clinical presentation and underlying pathobiology. LBD substantially impacts patient function, independence, and quality of life. Current therapies are symptomatic, and disease-modifying therapies are not established. Advances in in vivo biomarkers provide an important window for early disease diagnosis and intervention.
This review examines the complex spectrum of LBD, including DLB, PDD, and prodromal states of MCI-LB and PD-MCI. Advances in biomarkers and biological frameworks are considered along with limitations in DLB. Recent pharmacological and non-pharmacological clinical trials are highlighted. The authors offer commentary on the challenges and opportunities for current and future research and care in LBD.
LBD remains a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge. The development and validation of in vivo biomarkers of LBD permit improved and earlier diagnosis, along with deeper characterization of LBD. Further research is needed to harmonize and implement biological frameworks and staging, develop and validate biomarkers and LBD-relevant clinical outcome measures, and design clinical trials using biologically based agents for disease-modification. Lastly, creating holistic care plans that span the entire disease is essential for improving patient outcomes.

title: Predictors of Antiamyloid Medication Utilization and Adherence Among People With Alzheimer Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment.
abstract:
From 2021 to 2024, 3 amyloid monoclonal antibody medications (aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab) were approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for treatment of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild dementia due to Alzheimer disease (AD). We determined the demographics and social drivers of health associated with utilization and initial adherence of these medications.
We used the Vizient database to identify patients with MCI or dementia using an ICD-10 coding definition. Propensity score matching was used to match patients who received an antiamyloid medication to those who did not, based on date of MCI/dementia diagnosis and follow-up. Social drivers of health were assessed using the Vizient Vulnerability Index (VVI), a neighborhood-level measure of socioeconomic vulnerability. Logistic regression determined associations between demographics, Elixhauser comorbidity, and VVI, with utilization of antiamyloid medications. Poisson regression determined associations between demographic, Elixhauser comorbidity, and VVI and initial adherence (measured as days supplied) of antiamyloid medications.
We identified 1,198,362 participants with MCI/dementia, of whom 2,427 (0.2%) were prescribed an antiamyloid medication. Of those prescribed an antiamyloid medication, 1,696 (69.9%) were matched to participants with MCI/dementia that were not prescribed antiamyloid medications (mean age 75.5 [SD 9.5], 56.1% female, 80.1% non-Hispanic White). We found that higher age (odds ratio [OR] 0.93, 95% CI 0.92-0.94), higher Elixhauser comorbidity index (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.52-0.59), being non-Hispanic Black (OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.09-0.23), and being Hispanic (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.13-0.36) associated with lower odds of receiving an antiamyloid medication. Furthermore, having greater VVI was associated with lower odds of receiving an antiamyloid medication. By contrast, only higher Elixhauser comorbidity score was associated with lower initial medication adherence (rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.93-0.96), but not age, sex, race/ethnicity, and overall vulnerability.
We found that younger, non-Hispanic White patients, with fewer comorbidities, and lower vulnerability, were more likely to receive antiamyloid medications. By contrast, among patients receiving an antiamyloid medication, only higher comorbidity score associated with lower initial medication adherence. These findings indicate a potential disparity in medication access for US patients with MCI/dementia that could become problematic barriers to care as medications for dementia continue to evolve.

title: Potential links between PCOS/PMOS and Alzheimer disease and related dementias.
abstract:
Polycystic ovary syndrome/polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PCOS/PMOS) is a common endocrine disorder with significant metabolic and reproductive implications. Increasing attention has focused on its potential long-term neurological consequences, including possible links to cognitive impairment and Alzheimer disease (AD), through overlapping biological pathways.
We conducted a comprehensive PubMed search, from inception through October 2025, identifying studies on cognitive performance, brain structure and function, neurodegenerative biomarkers, and dementia risk in PCOS/PMOS patients.
Evidence supports multiple potential mechanistic pathways that could connect PCOS/PMOS to AD-relevant biology, such as insulin resistance (IR), chronic inflammation, hormonal dysregulation, and cardiovascular dysfunction. These pathways converge on neurodegeneration processes such as impaired Aβ clearance, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, and cerebral metabolic deficits. Clinically, PCOS/PMOS patients exhibit mild but reproducible impairments in executive function and memory, alongside structural and functional brain alterations, including hippocampal and white matter changes, and altered network connectivity. However, these findings are influenced by coexisting metabolic dysfunction, and direct epidemiological evidence linking PCOS/PMOS to increased dementia incidence remains limited and inconsistent.
Current evidence indicates that any association between PCOS/PMOS and AD risk is likely mediated by metabolic comorbidities, particularly IR and obesity, rather than an independent effect of PCOS/PMOS itself. However, clinical evidence for increased PCOS/PMOS risk for cognitive vulnerability and dementia remain inconsistent and cognitive benefits from PCOS/PMOS-specific interventions are lacking. Clinical focus should therefore remain on optimizing metabolic health, while longitudinal and interventional studies are required to clarify long-term neurological relationships and outcomes.

title: p53 deficiency increases vulnerability to chronic stress-induced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors: Role of calcium dysregulation and BDNF signaling.
abstract: The tumor suppressor protein p53 is a known modulator of neurodegenerative disease (ND) processes. Although p53 expression is increased in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and ischemic stroke, its role in mood disorders such as anxiety and depression remains unclear. To investigate the role of p53 in behavioral responses to chronic stress, we examined behavioral and molecular alterations in p53 knockout (p53-/-) mice and wild type mice. In p53-/- mice, increased vulnerability to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors was observed following CUMS exposure. In parallel with these behavioral changes, BDNF expression was reduced, whereas glutamate levels were elevated in the prefrontal cortex of p53-/- mice. Increased calcium-associated staining and NMDAR2B expression were observed together with increased neuronal injury- and cell death-related markers. In primary cortical neurons derived from p53-/- mice, corticosterone treatment resulted in greater increases in glutamate levels, NMDAR2B expression compared to wild-type controls. Cell death markers (cleaved caspase-3, p-p38, p-JNK) were upregulated, while neuroprotective signals (BDNF, p-Akt, p-ERK, p-CREB) were suppressed in p53-/- mice, and corticosterone-treated primary neuronal cells from p53-/- mice. These findings indicate that p53 deficiency is associated with enhanced vulnerability to CUMS-induced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors and is accompanied by alterations in calcium handling, glutamate homeostasis, neuronal injury-related markers, and BDNF-associated neuroprotective signaling.

title: Dysregulated Metal Homeostasis in Alzheimer's Disease: From Pathological Modulators to Therapeutic Targets.
abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.

title: A natural neuronal receptor-derived MRI probe targets β-amyloid oligomers for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Early-to-mid detection of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains challenging because clinically used amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) probes primarily visualize fibrillar β-amyloid (Aβ) deposits and require radioactive isotopes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers a radiation-free alternative, but its application in molecular AD diagnosis is limited by insufficient blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration and poor specificity toward early-to-mid Aβ species. Here, we developed a BBB-crossing liposomal MRI probe, Lipo@D1D2-Gd, by integrating a natural Aβ oligomer-binding receptor domain with a gadolinium chelator. The extracellular D1D2 domains of human leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor B2 (LilrB2), a neuronal receptor that recognizes neurotoxic Aβ oligomers, were recombinantly produced and bioorthogonally conjugated with a gadolinium chelator. The resulting D1D2-Gd retained its Aβ-binding capability and MRI contrast activity. To enable brain delivery, D1D2-Gd was encapsulated within maltose-functionalized PEGylated liposomes designed to facilitate BBB transport. After intravenous administration to 4-month-old 5xFAD mice, Lipo@D1D2-Gd crossed the BBB, accumulated in Aβ-rich brain regions, and generated MRI contrast enhancement that differentiated 5xFAD mice from wild-type controls. Systemic safety evaluation showed no obvious hematological, biochemical, or histological toxicity. This study establishes a receptor-derived, BBB-crossing biomaterial platform for radiation-free molecular imaging of early-to-mid AD-associated Aβ pathology. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: 1) Promising Targeting Strategy: We repurposed a human-derived natural receptor domain (LilrB2 D1D2) as a targeting module for β-amyloid (Aβ) oligomers, a key pathogenic species in Alzheimer's disease (AD). 2) Non-invasive MRI Approach: We constructed a liposomal probe designed to deliver the Gd-labeled targeting agent to the brain, enabling the detection of Aβ-associated pathology in 4-month-old 5xFAD mice via non-radioactive MRI, well before overt cognitive decline. 3) Experimental Validation: We demonstrate the probe's association with Aβ oligomers/plaques, effective BBB crossing, differences in MRI signals between AD model and wild-type mice, and an initially favorable biosafety profile, with no observed toxicity under the tested conditions. 4) Clinical Translation Potential: Our work presents a promising pathway toward a safe, accessible, and early-to-mid-stage AD screening tool, with the potential to facilitate population-wide screening and earlier therapeutic intervention.

title: Regional atrophy and hypoperfusion mediate the association between affective symptoms and cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract:
Affective symptoms are common and associated with poor cognitive outcomes in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, their underlying neural correlations remain poorly understood.
This study included 105 patients with AD. Patients were classified into an AD with affective symptoms (AD-A) group and an AD without affective symptoms (AD-NA) group according to scores obtained on the depression and anxiety items of the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. All of the participants underwent neuropsychological assessments and multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans.
Compared with the AD-NA group, the AD-A group was younger and exhibited more severe, widespread cognitive impairments. Neuroimaging revealed that the AD-A group exhibited reduced grey matter volume (GMV) in the bilateral posterior cerebellum and right fusiform gyrus, along with reduced global cerebral blood flow (CBF) and lower CBF in the left parieto-temporo-occipital region. Mediation analyses revealed significant indirect associations between affective symptoms and cognitive function via cerebellar GMV and left parieto-temporo-occipital CBF.
Cerebellar structural atrophy and left parieto-temporo-occipital hypoperfusion are associated with both affective symptoms and cognitive impairment and may represent neural correlates of the affective-cognitive association in AD patients.

title: Therapeutic targeting of G protein-coupled receptors in central nervous system disorders: from novel mechanisms to precision pharmacology.
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major therapeutic targets for central nervous system disorders, with more than 500 approved drugs targeting this receptor family worldwide. This review comprehensively examines the pathophysiological roles and therapeutic potential of GPCRs in major neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and depression. We highlight how dysregulated signaling through specific GPCRs, including dopamine and adenosine A2A receptors in PD, the mGlu5 receptor and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in AD, S1P and GPR17 receptors in MS, and 5-HT1A and GPR39 receptors in depression, contributes to disease pathogenesis. Beyond canonical monomeric activation, this review emphasizes emerging concepts in GPCR heterodimerization (e.g., the 5-HT1A/orexin 1 receptor complex activating Gαs pathways), biased signaling, and allosteric modulation, which provide opportunities to develop therapeutics with greater specificity and fewer adverse effects. We also evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting these mechanisms using specific pharmacological agents, including synthetic compounds and structurally defined natural product-derived molecules. The chemical structures of key natural products-including paeoniflorin, rosmarinic acid, and ergothioneine-are presented, with their GPCR interactions and critical pharmacophores highlighted. Finally, we discuss future directions involving advanced technologies, including cryo-electron microscopy, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids, structural biology, and artificial intelligence, to improve understanding of complex GPCR signaling. The development of biased ligands, stage-specific interventions, and GPCR-based biomarkers represents a critical step toward personalized and more effective treatments for neurological disorders.

title: STAT3 mediated the isoleucine-induced Alzheimer's disease progression.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that significantly impacts millions globally, with rising prevalence among the aging population, emphasizing the need for effective interventions. Isoleucine, a branched-chain amino acid, crosses the blood-brain barrier and plays a role in various neurological disorders. In this study, we investigated the association of isoleucine with AD traits using the BXD mouse reference population, revealing significant correlations with Y-maze performance, anxiety assays, contextual fear conditioning, and the age of onset for working memory deficits. In vitro, exogenous isoleucine supplementation in HT22 and PC12 cells increased amyloid precursor protein (APP) and phosphorylated tau (p-tau) levels. Subsequent analysis identified 2,000 probes correlated with isoleucine and revealed STAT3 as a candidate downstream regulator. Overexpression of STAT3 increased APP and p-tau levels, and STAT3 inhibition abolished this effect, suggesting that isoleucine modulates AD progression via STAT3 activation. Mendelian randomization analysis further supported a causal relationship between elevated isoleucine levels and AD risk. This work provides insights into isoleucine as a potential risk factor for AD and identifies STAT3 as a mediator of isoleucine-related AD susceptibility.

title: From Clinical Manifestations to Neural Mechanisms: A Systematic Review of Neurobehavioral Consequences of Pregabalin Misuse and Abuse.
abstract:
Pregabalin is a γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) analog. It is prescribed for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, anxiety disorders, and seizures. Pregabalin misuse and abuse have increased rapidly worldwide in recent years, raising public concerns owing to its addictive potential and associated neurotoxicity. To systematically characterize the neurobehavioral effects of pregabalin misuse and abuse, recent research was synthesized, and the relevant literature was reviewed to identify key findings, explore limitations, and outline future directions.
This systematic review followed the PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CNKI, and Wanfang were searched for literature covering case series, cross-sectional, prospective, and retrospective studies, and animal experiments. The study's focus was to synthesize evidence of the neurobehavioral consequences of pregabalin misuse and abuse, and explore the association between clinical symptoms and neurobiological mechanisms.
A total of 23 studies met the inclusion criteria. Acute overdose consistently produced neuroinhibitory symptoms and reward-seeking behaviors. Repeated or chronic exposure was associated with dose-dependent cognitive impairment, psychiatric comorbidity, addiction, and withdrawal syndrome. Preclinical studies revealed dopaminergic dysregulation, oxidative stress, and neuroadaptive remodeling.
Human evidence consistently links acute overdose to neuroinhibitory symptoms and reward-seeking behaviors, with severity correlating with dose. Preclinical studies provide a plausible mechanistic hypothesis: acute pregabalin exposure may activate mesolimbic dopamine signaling while chronic high-dose exposure is associated with monoamine disruption, oxidative stress, inflammatory activation, and receptor remodeling in animal models. Direct translation of these findings to human pathophysiology warrants further investigation.
Pregabalin misuse and abuse is associated with serious neurobehavioral risks, including acute neurotoxicity, chronic cognitive and psychiatric impairment, and addiction risk. However, the evidence base remains limited, and causal inference is constrained by the predominance of observational human studies and the preliminary nature of animal mechanistic data. Further research should refine risk stratification and inform public health strategies for early identification and intervention.

title: Depression and anxiety among older surgical patients with cognitive impairment: a multicenter longitudinal cohort study.
abstract:
Cognitive impairment (CI), depression, and anxiety are underrecognized yet frequently co-existing conditions linked to poor surgical outcomes in older patients. We examined: 1) the prevalence and perioperative trajectory of depression/anxiety in patients with and without CI; 2) preoperative patient-reported outcome measures; and 3) postoperative outcomes associated with depression/anxiety.
This study included 369 surgical patients (≥65 years) from two academic tertiary care hospitals. CI was assessed with the Ascertain Dementia Eight preoperatively, while depression/anxiety was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 preoperatively, at 30-, and 90 days postoperatively. The trajectory of depression/anxiety in CI versus no-CI patients was analyzed with linear mixed-effects models.
Preoperatively, 28% of patients had depression/anxiety, 13% had CI, and 8% had co-existing depression/anxiety and CI. Those with depression/anxiety were more likely to have co-existing CI than those without depression/anxiety (29% vs. 6%; P<0.001). Patients that screened positive for preoperative CI experienced significantly worse psychological symptoms at all times compared to those without CI. Among those with preoperative CI, mean psychological symptoms remained above screening thresholds for depression/anxiety at all time points and significantly worsened at 90 days post-surgery compared to baseline levels. Patients with depression/anxiety reported significantly worse preoperative health, including greater pain and functional disability, as well as worse quality of life and sleep.
Given greater psychological burden in those with CI, screening for both conditions may enable early identification of patients at higher risk for poor outcomes. This approach may ultimately enhance risk stratification and optimization of perioperative care in older adults.

title: Evening chronotype and incidence of all-cause dementia and subtypes after accounting for other sleep traits: A prospective cohort study.
abstract: BackgroundChronotype may affect neurophysiology, but whether its association with dementia persists independent of other sleep traits remains uncertain.ObjectiveTo examine associations of chronotype with incident dementia subtypes and potential modification by metabolic and social factors.MethodsIn 443,906 dementia-free participants, Cox models estimated dementia risk after adjustment for sociodemographic, lifestyle, clinical, apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype, and sleep-related factors. We tested baseline interactions and robustness using multiple imputation, competing-risk models, and landmark analyses.ResultsOver a mean follow-up of 12.5 years, 6355 incident dementia cases were documented. Evening chronotype was associated with a small increased risk of all-cause dementia compared with morning types (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01-1.14). This association was observed primarily in "other dementias" (HR, 1.12; 1.04-1.21), with no significant association with Alzheimer's disease or vascular dementia (VaD).Exploratory subgroup analyses identified two interactions that remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction: social visit frequency for all-cause dementia and napping for VaD (FDR-adjusted p for interaction is 0.024 for both). Evening chronotype was associated with higher all-cause dementia risk among participants reporting infrequent social visits and with higher VaD risk among those reporting usual napping.ConclusionsEvening chronotype was associated with a small increase in the hazard of all-cause dementia after multivariable adjustment. Given the modest magnitude and observational design, evening chronotype may be considered a potential risk marker rather than an independent or causal risk factor. These findings require independent replication.

title: A comprehensive review of the neurobehavioral and neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q in fish, rodents, and humans.
abstract: N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD) is a widely used tire additive that undergoes environmental transformation to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), which is ubiquitously detected in environmental matrices. Increasing evidence demonstrates that exposure to 6PPD-Q adversely affects organisms through neurobehavioral disruption and neurotoxicity. While studies document behavioral abnormalities and molecular alterations, a comprehensive synthesis linking these outcomes remains limited. The objective of this review was to synthesize current literature reporting neurobehavioral and neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q in fish, rodents, and humans using experimental and computational approaches. Using PRISMA guidelines, a search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar using several key phrases related to 6PPD-Q and neurotoxicity, capturing 1874 records. Relevant articles were assessed by full-text review for criteria eligibility, and the final review included 27 articles. In fish, exposure to 6PPD-Q can alter neurobehaviors like locomotor activity, anxiety-like responses, social and aggressive behaviors, and disturbances in circadian-regulated activities. Such behavioral outcomes correspond closely with neurotransmitter imbalance, neuroendocrine disruption, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and transcriptome changes affecting neural signaling pathways. In rodents, repeated or chronic exposure to 6PPD-Q leads to neuronal damage, cognitive impairment, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits. Human biomonitoring and mechanistic studies further associate 6PPD-Q exposure with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and molecular responses relevant to neurological diseases. Leveraging the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database, computational analysis revealed entities associated with 6PPD-Q in the database were related to Alzheimer's disease, dopaminergic synapses, neurotrophin signaling pathways, and Parkinson's disease. Taken together, data suggests that 6PPD-Q may interfere with neuronal signaling, connectivity, and plasticity, leading to behavioral deficits. Based on predictive docking scores using fish, rodent, and human orthologs, 6PPD-Q may interact with tyrosine hydroxylase and L-dopa decarboxylase which can potentially lead to disrupted dopamine biosynthesis pathways. Given the widespread environmental presence of 6PPD-Q and its continuous introduction into aquatic ecosystems, characterizing such mechanisms is critical for improving ecological and human health risk assessments.

title: Genetic correlates of corticobasal degeneration: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
Corticobasal degeneration (CBD) is a primary 4-repeat tauopathy marked by progressive motor, cognitive, and behavioral decline, substantial clinicopathologic heterogeneity, and few disease-modifying therapeutic options. Although MAPT variation has long been implicated in CBD susceptibility, the full genetic architecture of CBD has remained highly fragmented and poorly synthesized.
This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines to identify studies evaluating genetic associations with CBD through August 2026. Eligible studies reported effect estimates for MAPT haplotypes, MAPT subhaplotypes, MAPT SNPs, or non-MAPT candidate loci. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-E, and pooled associations were calculated using inverse-variance meta-analysis. Twenty-two studies published between 2001 and 2025 were included.
The most consistent associations involved MAPT haplotype architecture, with H1 and H1/H1 showing increased CBD susceptibility and H2 showing a protective association. Among MAPT H1 subhaplotypes, H1c, H1d, and H1q demonstrated significant risk associations, whereas other subhaplotypes showed less significant effects. MAPT SNP-level associations were generally modest, though several variants showed small yet significant protective or risk-related effects. Among non-MAPT loci, C9orf72, MOBP, and KIF13B were associated with CBD risk.
These results indicate that genetic susceptibility to CBD is dominated by MAPT architecture; however, significant heterogeneity within and beyond MAPT exists, with significant contributions from select subhaplotypes, SNPs, and non-MAPT loci. Overall, these findings support tau-centered genetic vulnerability while highlighting candidate pathways relevant to CBD pathogenesis, glial biology, and broader neurodegenerative vulnerability, providing a foundation for future biomarker, mechanistic, and precision-medicine studies.

title: Sublexical compensatory reorganization of Chinese character recognition in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract:
This study investigated the cognitive-functional shift in visual character recognition across the cognitive decline trajectory, ranging from healthy aging through Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Mild Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Specifically, it was hypothesized that as global semantic networks degrade, the reliance on rapid holistic processing decreases, prompting a compensatory shift toward sublexical features.
Using a controlled unmasked priming lexical decision paradigm, this study evaluated behavioral performance across three distinct participant groups (N = 30 per group): healthy controls (HC), individuals with MCI, and patients with Mild AD. The experimental stimuli consisted of 80 Chinese phonograms matched across key psycholinguistic properties. This study utilized mixed-design Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) alongside item-level hierarchical multiple regression (HMR) models to isolate the specific drivers of reaction times, assessing the predictive power of visual complexity, whole-character frequency, semantic transparency, and phonetic regularity.
The analytical models revealed distinctly divergent psycholinguistic trajectories. The HC group demonstrated highly efficient holistic processing, with performance primarily driven by whole-character frequency. Conversely, the MCI group exhibited a unique transitional cognitive profile, characterized by a simultaneous reliance on both holistic whole-word access and analytic sublexical features. Crucially, in the Mild AD tgroup, the holistic processing advantage was entirely abolished. This functional disintegration triggered a compensatory reorganization toward bottom-up sublexical properties, with patients relying heavily on semantic transparency and phonetic regularity to achieve semantic access.
These findings demonstrate a linguistic Compensation-Related Utilization of Neural Circuits Hypothesis (CRUNCH) effect within the degenerating brain. As top-down lexical-semantic hubs deteriorate, reflected behaviorally in this paradigm by the loss of holistic processing advantages, the cognitive system actively compensates by upregulating bottom-up, sublexical pathways. Furthermore, the transitional sublexical dependency observed during the MCI stage highlights the translational potential of psycholinguistic variables as sensitive, noninvasive behavioral biomarkers for the early screening and monitoring of dementia.

title: Gene-based association analysis of depression risk among European ancestry Parkinson's disease patients.
abstract: Depression is one of the most common and disabling non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its genetic basis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the genetic contributions to depression in PD by estimating the burden from common as well as low-frequency single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within genes previously implicated in PD or depression risk among European ancestry PD patients from three population-based studies. Using gene-based association analyses (SKAT, Burden, and SKAT-O) in the PASIDA, PEG, and PPMI studies, we evaluated SNP sets in gene regions previously linked to PD or depression. Among PD-related genes, meta-analysis identified a significant association between KRTCAP2 and self-reported depression diagnosis in PD (SKAT-O p = 4.33 × 10⁻⁵), which remained significant after false discovery rate correction. A higher genetic burden in KRTCAP2 was associated with 20% increased odds of depression (OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.04-1.38). TRAF5 and LRRK2 showed marginal associations. Among depression-related genes, SPPL3 and ERBB4 were associated with depression diagnosis history, and FNIP2 was associated with current depressive symptoms. The PD polygenic risk score was not associated with depression in PD, while a higher depression polygenic risk score was significantly associated with increased odds of depression diagnosis in both cohorts and the meta-analysis (OR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.13-1.40). Our findings highlight immune-related genes such as KRTCAP2 and TRAF5 as potential contributors to depression in PD. Additionally, the depression PRS shows statistically significant association with depression diagnosis in PD, suggesting that a general depression-related genetic liability contributes to this non-motor feature in PD. Together, these results suggest that depression in PD may involve both shared and disease-specific genetic mechanisms, offering new insights into its pathogenesis and potential therapeutic targets.

title: GBA1 Canada initiative (G-can), a pre-competitive, open science platform for GBA1 research.
abstract: GBA1 Canada (G-Can) is a pre-competitive, open-science platform serving as a central hub for basic, translational, and clinical research on GBA1, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme acid beta-glucocerebrosidase (GCase), a key component of the glycosphingolipid metabolism pathway. G-Can unites basic scientists, clinicians, and industry partners in Canada and internationally to minimize duplication of effort and maximize research impact. G-Can has established a comprehensive and growing suite of biological, clinical, and analytical resources for the GBA1 research community. Through the C-BIG Repository and partner infrastructures, these resources are made broadly accessible to academic and industry investigators under non-exclusive agreements, in accordance with G-Can's open-science mandate. G-Can's primary objectives are to deepen understanding of GCase biology and its genetic modifiers, validate disease-relevant biomarkers, and establish trial-ready cohorts exceeding 5000 genotyped participants. Therapeutic programs under development include gene therapy, RNA-based approaches, and combination strategies, with a Phase 0/1 clinical trial targeted within five years. By integrating open-science infrastructure with coordinated therapeutic development, G-Can aims to accelerate the translation of discovery into clinical application for patients with GBA1-associated neurodegeneration.

title: Risk factors for suicidal behaviour in people with dementia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
Dementia-related affective symptoms and social withdrawal increase vulnerability to suicidal behaviour. This study evaluates the magnitude of this risk and its determinants, focusing specifically on suicide attempts and deaths.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies was conducted. Eight English- and Chinese-language databases were searched from inception to May 2025. Pooled odds ratios (OR) were estimated using random-effects models to compare people with dementia (PwD) with controls and to identify risk factors within the dementia population.
Thirty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria. Dementia was associated with a 62% increased risk of suicidal behaviour compared with non-dementia controls (pooled OR = 1.62; 95% CI 1.32-1.98). Risk was notably concentrated in specific subgroups: younger patients were nearly three times more likely to die by suicide than older patients, and men faced 28% higher odds of suicide attempts and 188% increased odds of suicide deaths compared to women. Social isolation and psychiatric history-particularly depression-were robust risk markers. Notably, the exhaustive search of Chinese-language databases yielded no eligible publications, revealing a significant geographical evidence gap.
PwD face a significant increase in suicidal behaviour, concentrated within subgroups with psychiatric and social vulnerabilities. Prevention should prioritise younger patients, men, and socially isolated individuals. The identified lack of diverse data necessitates future cross-cultural qualitative research in English and Chinese to bridge the gap between Western and Eastern perspectives and capture culturally situated risk factors currently missing from the literature.

title: Multidimensional Clinical Benefits of Cinnamon Leaf Oil Inhalation in Primary and Metastatic Brain Tumor Patients During Winter: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
To evaluate the multidimensional efficacy of 12‑week cinnamon leaf oil (CLO) inhalation as a seasonal adjuvant supportive‑care intervention for alleviating winter‑exacerbated non‑motor symptom burden and improving mood disorders, sleep quality, refractory fatigue, and functional independence in patients with primary and metastatic brain tumors.
This randomized, controlled clinical trial enrolled 328 patients diagnosed with primary or metastatic brain tumors, randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to intervention group (standard antitumor care plus 12‑week undiluted CLO inhalation, 2h/day, 5 days/week, n=165) or control group (standard care plus distilled‑water‑vapor sham‑aromatherapy control, n=163). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were descriptively summarized for both groups. The primary outcome was the change in HAM-D total score from baseline to week 12. Secondary outcome indicators included changes in anxiety (HAM‑A), sleep quality (PSQI), physical/mental fatigue (FS-14), and activities of daily living (ADL-BI). Integrated multidimensional outcome profiling was further performed to examine changes across six clinical domains.
Twelve weeks of CLO inhalation was associated with improvements across the assessed outcome measures, whereas the control group receiving only standard care showed minimal clinical changes. The intervention group showed reductions in emotional symptoms, with HAM‑A scores decreasing from 17.65±4.48 to 12.25±4.51 (p<0.001) and HAM‑D scores declining from 22.10±5.41 to 13.68±2.71 (p<0.001). Improvements in sleep quality were observed, with PSQI total scores dropping from 12.18±3.05 to 5.25±1.86 (p<0.01). Additionally, the CLO group showed changes in functional independence, with ADL‑BI total scores increasing from 63.60±14.16 to 74.88±11.33 (p<0.01). In terms of fatigue relief, the proportions of patients with severe physical and mental fatigue decreased by 46% and 76%, respectively (p<0.01). Multidimensional profiling indicated favourable changes for CLO inhalation across sleep, anxiety, depression, physical fatigue remission, mental fatigue remission and daily function. Only mild Grade 1 transient mucosal irritation adverse events occurred in the intervention group with low incidence; no severe adverse reactions or trial withdrawal were observed.
Findings from this single‑centre trial suggest that 12‑week standardized CLO inhalation may represent a tolerable non‑pharmacological adjuvant approach for brain tumour patients. It was associated with reductions in winter‑exacerbated anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, and refractory fatigue, as well as improvements in patients' functional independence. Observations of multi‑domain symptom changes warrant further clinical investigation to evaluate its utility within neuro‑oncological supportive‑care practice and patients' long‑term quality‑of‑life outcomes.

title: Assessment of change in drug-induced parkinsonism in daily-life gait using vision-based machine learning.
abstract: Drug-induced parkinsonism is a potentially reversible movement disorder that may be subtle and difficult to monitor in residential dementia care. Vision-based machine learning analysis of gait may provide unobtrusive longitudinal monitoring around medication changes. We conducted a two-center cohort study of 61 residents with dementia receiving psychotropic medication. Hallway gait sequences were recorded using ceiling-mounted cameras and converted to three-dimensional body pose. A TabPFN classifier estimated UPDRS-III item 29 gait severity for each walk. We evaluated associations between acute antipsychotic (AP) and antidepressant (AD) dose reduction/cessation (≥50% dose reduction or cessation, 0-21 days after change) and daily mean predicted gait severity using linear mixed-effects models in ever-exposed participants, with complementary equal-weight paired analyses among participants observed in both medication states. In mixed-effects models, acute AP dose reduction/cessation was associated with lower predicted gait severity (β=-0.127, p = 0.022), whereas AD dose reduction/cessation was not (β=-0.060, p = 0.210). Equal-weight paired analyses found no statistically significant participant-average within-person change among paired participants (AP mean change = 0.031, 95% CI [-0.114, 0.176], p = 0.653; AD mean change =-0.021, 95% CI [-0.098, 0.056], p = 0.575), consistent with heterogeneous individual responses. Vision-based monitoring captured within-participant gait variation around psychotropic dose-reduction periods, but findings are associative. Larger prospective studies with documented reasons for medication changes are needed before using such monitoring to guide medication decisions.

title: Antidepressants and cognitive function in major depressive disorder: Mechanisms, clinical evidence, and implications for precision treatment.
abstract: Cognitive impairment is a core feature of major depressive disorder (MDD) and significantly impairs functional recovery. This review summarizes current evidence on the effects of antidepressants on cognitive function and discusses the underlying mechanisms. Antidepressants may exert their effects through multiple mechanisms, including modulation of monoaminergic neurotransmission, enhancement of neuroplasticity, and regulation of stress and inflammatory pathways. Available studies indicate that antidepressants differ in their cognitive benefits, with vortioxetine showing the most consistent procognitive evidence. Duloxetine, bupropion, and some augmentation strategies may also improve specific cognitive domains, though the evidence is limited. Importantly, cognitive improvement may result from direct drug effects on cognition or indirectly via alleviation of depressive symptoms, highlighting the need for mediation analyses in future research. In patients with late-life depression, vortioxetine and duloxetine have shown relatively clear benefits, and augmentation with cognitive enhancers has demonstrated some potential. The long-term cognitive protective effects of antidepressants remain unconfirmed. Immuno-metabolic depression subtypes, high-dose-related adverse effects, and comorbidity with anxiety and sleep disorders may constitute important sources of residual cognitive deficits. Emerging treatments such as ketamine, psychedelic compounds, and interventions targeting the gut-brain axis may offer new opportunities for addressing cognitive dysfunction in MDD. Current evidence is limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneous cognitive assessments. Future research should prioritize large, randomized controlled trials with cognition as the primary endpoint, using standardized assessment tools. A better understanding of the cognitive profiles and mechanisms of antidepressants may support precision medicine strategies and promote functional recovery in patients with MDD.

title: Aberrant amygdala subregion volumes in youth at high risk for bipolar disorder predict antidepressant-induced adverse events.
abstract: Youth with familial risk for bipolar disorder (BD) and current depression/anxiety are vulnerable to antidepressant-induced adverse events (AE), including mania. The amygdala, implicated in the pathophysiology of mood disorders, may play a key role in these AE. 105 youth with at least one first-degree relative with BD-I and a current depressive/anxiety disorder (high-risk) and 51 healthy controls (HC) underwent baseline MRI to investigate neurostructural risk factors for antidepressant-induced AE. High-risk youth were randomized to either psychotherapy plus escitalopram or psychotherapy plus placebo (2:1) for up to 16 weeks. Clinical efficacy was assessed using the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised and Pediatric Anxiety Rating Scale, and AE were assessed using the Pediatric Adverse Events Rating Scale and Treatment-Emergent Activation and Suicidality Assessment Profile. Baseline amygdala subregion volumes and their associations with the rates of change in clinical symptoms and AE over time were evaluated using linear regression models. Compared to HC, high-risk youth had reduced volumes in left lateral and medial nuclei, bilateral central and cortical nuclei, and bilateral corticoamygdaloid transition area and increased volumes in bilateral basal and accessory basal nuclei. In escitalopram-treated youth, but not those receiving placebo, smaller baseline volumes in bilateral cortical nuclei and left medial nucleus were associated with fewer arousal-related AE. Additionally, larger bilateral basal nuclei volumes at baseline were associated with more arousal-related AE. Widespread amygdala volume abnormalities provide insights into neurobiological mechanisms underlying the development of BD in high-risk youth, and specific subregion volumes may serve as neurostructural markers for predicting antidepressant-induced AE.

title: Neuronavigated dual-target transcranial magnetic stimulation for schizophrenia negative symptoms.
abstract: Negative symptoms in schizophrenia severely impair function and quality of life, yet respond poorly to current therapies. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of neuronavigated dual-target repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and cerebellum for improving negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04853485). Participants with first-episode schizophrenia or clinical high-risk for psychosis were enrolled from Shanghai Mental Health Center and Suzhou Guangji Hospital. Participants were randomly assigned to either a real or sham group under MRI-guided neuronavigation, targeting rDLPFC with 1Hz at 100% motor threshold(MT), cerebellar with intermittent theta burst stimulation(iTBS) at 120% MT for 20 consecutive days. Clinical assessments were conducted at baseline(T0), 10-session(T1), 20-session(T2) and one month after the intervention(T3). Cognition and MRI were evaluated at T0 and T2. The primary outcome was change of negative subscale score of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale(PANSS), while secondary outcomes included alterations in other PANSS subscale scores and fronto-cerebellar circuit functional connectivity. In total, 75 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (36 active, 39 sham). The pre-specified primary linear mixed-effects analysis revealed a non-significant group-by-time interaction for PANSS negative subscale scores (F(3,174.6)=1.45, p=0.230). At the 4-week endpoint (T2), the nominal unadjusted between-group p-value was 0.049; after Sidak correction for multiple comparisons, the adjusted mean difference was -2.48 points (95% CI -4.99 to 0.03, adjusted p=0.150, Cohen's d=-0.51). Descriptive uncorrected t-tests indicated greater negative-symptom reductions in the active group at T1 and T2, and the 4-week negative-symptom response rate (≥50% reduction) was higher under real rTMS (χ2=9.5, p=0.002). A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for PANSS positive subscale scores (F(3,172.0)=3.26, p=0.023). Both groups exhibited substantial within-group symptom improvement. Resting-state fMRI demonstrated group-by-time interactions within cerebello-temporal, parahippocampal, caudate, and parietal networks (FWE-corrected p<0.05), and negative-symptom change correlated with cerebello-caudate connectivity (r=0.33, p=0.026). These findings suggest neuronavigated dual-target rTMS over rDLPFC and cerebellum may be associated with numerical improvements in negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis.

title: Frontiers in Neurotransmitter Probes: Innovations and Perspectives in Norepinephrine Detection Technology.
abstract: Norepinephrine (NE), the primary neurotransmitter of locus coeruleus projections, plays a crucial role in regulating arousal, emotion, memory, and stress responses. Its dysregulation is closely associated with various neurological disorders such as depression, Parkinson's disease, and epilepsy. However, conventional detection techniques such as microdialysis coupled with liquid chromatography are constrained by limited spatiotemporal resolution and inherent invasiveness, largely due to NE's low concentration, rapid metabolism, and complex distribution in vivo. These limitations make real-time, in situ dynamic monitoring particularly challenging. In recent years, fluorescence and bioluminescence probe technologies, founded on molecular recognition or self-assembly strategies, have enabled notable advances in the in situ detection and imaging of NE, owing to their superior spatiotemporal resolution, favorable biocompatibility, and versatile design. This review summarizes several representative studies in the field, covering probe design principles, response mechanisms, analytical performance, and biological applications. It also highlights emerging frontiers such as subcellular localization, in vivo dynamic imaging, millisecond-scale monitoring, multitarget cooperative recognition, and integrated diagnosis and therapy. These technologies have deepened our understanding of the spatiotemporal dynamics of NE in physiological and pathological processes, while also providing powerful tools for mechanistic research, early diagnosis, and precise treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders.
