title: Apathy in normal pressure hydrocephalus: frequency, clinical correlates, and relationship to cerebrospinal fluid removal response.
abstract: Apathy is a highly prevalent neuropsychiatric feature of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), but its clinical correlates and relevance to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) removal trial response are poorly understood. We evaluated 161 adults with possible or probable NPH whose informants completed the Frontal Systems Behavior Scale (FrSBe), which provides normative ratings for premorbid (i.e. before symptom onset) and current apathy. Apathy change was defined as current minus premorbid ratings of apathy. Among the sample, 69.6% showed clinically elevated apathy (T-score ≥ 65) compared to 18.0% premorbidly; 91.9% showed increased apathy (Mean T-Score Change = 25.5, p < .001, d = 1.29). Partial Spearman correlations (controlling for cognitive symptom duration and depression) examined associations between apathy and gait, neuropsychological, functional, and disability measures. Gait responders were defined by clinical change in ≥2 gait measures post CSF-removal. The strongest correlates with apathy and apathy change were the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (ρ = .707 and .614) and the Quick Dementia Rating System (ρ = .682 and .587). Gait and cognitive composites (attention/speed/executive, overall) showed weaker (|ρ| = .208-.418) associations. Neither apathy nor apathy change differed between gait responders (n = 87) and non-responders (n = 48). Apathy is common in NPH and is related to disability and functional severity. It should therefore be routinely assessed in NPH evaluations.

title: Anti-N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptor Encephalitis With Autonomic Instability and Focal Seizures Without Detectable Ovarian Teratoma.
abstract: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis is a severe but potentially reversible form of autoimmune encephalitis, and it typically affects young women. It can be challenging to differentiate from other conditions that cause symptoms such as seizures and psychiatric and autonomic manifestations. We present the case of a previously healthy young woman without any significant past medical history who developed acute-onset, progressive neuropsychiatric disturbance, focal impaired awareness seizures, cognitive impairment, and intermittent autonomic disturbance manifesting as sinus tachycardia. Initial investigations showed mild pleocytosis in the CSF and subtle hyperintensity involving the right insular region and adjacent subcortical white matter on MRI. Further tests detected anti-NMDAR antibodies in both serum and CSF. She was started on first-line treatment with IV methylprednisolone and IVIG, but persistent cognitive impairment prompted escalation to second-line treatment with rituximab. She also underwent an extensive workup for an underlying ovarian teratoma or other neoplasms, including pelvic ultrasound and MRI, both of which were unremarkable. The patient eventually experienced gradual neurological recovery with immunotherapy and neurorehabilitation, ultimately regaining her independence and returning home. This case highlights autonomic dysfunction as a possible feature of anti-NMDAR encephalitis and the importance of early immunotherapy, even in patients without an identifiable tumor.

title: Neurotoxicity of Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics in Urinary Tract Infections: Mechanisms and Clinical Implications.
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) remain among the most common bacterial infections worldwide, affecting millions every year. While Escherichia coli (E. coli) is the predominant pathogen, a broad range of Gram-negative and Gram-positive organisms can be implicated. Treating UTIs, particularly complicated or severe infections, frequently relies on broad-spectrum antibiotics, often started empirically before identifying the causative pathogen. However, despite their ability to cover a wide spectrum of pathogens, they have become a growing threat to public health, mainly due to the rise of antimicrobial resistance, but also due to the many other adverse effects they can potentially cause. Neurotoxicity represents one of the most consequential yet underrecognized complications of antibiotic therapy. Broad-spectrum agents commonly used for UTIs, including fosfomycin, fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, and cephalosporins, have been associated with a wide range of neurologic manifestations such as epileptic seizures, encephalopathy, movement disorders, delirium, and psychosis, varying in onset, duration, severity, and reversibility. To induce such reactions, antibiotics interact with the central nervous system (CNS) in several ways that can threaten its integrity and disrupt homeostatic control of its components. This review provides a synopsis of the known neurological adverse reactions linked to four major antibiotic classes routinely used in UTI management and the mechanistic pathways underlying CNS toxicity. An overall clearer understanding of these risks may help clinicians balance therapeutic benefit against potential harm, optimize antimicrobial selection, and improve prevention and management strategies for antibiotic-associated neurotoxicity.

title: Gut Microbiota Modulation in CNS Disorders: Therapeutic Strategies and Implications for Drug Efficacy.
abstract: Various central nervous system (CNS) disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases, depression, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and anxiety, present significant obstacles to public health because of their intricate causes and the scarcity of effective treatments. Recent studies have shown that gut microbiota (GM) and CNS communicate bidirectionally. Modulation of immune system, neurotransmitters, and neuroactive metabolites are only a few examples of how GM can significantly influence CNS. Dysbiosis or changes in composition and function of gut microbes play a contributing role in various CNS disorders. In these disorders, probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, antibiotics use, and interventions based on microbial metabolites have demonstrated beneficial effects in animal models and some clinical studies. By restoring microbial equilibrium, increasing microbial diversity, and promoting the generation of beneficial metabolites, these approaches can improve the efficacy of traditional medications while minimizing their side effects and the disease itself, based on preclinical evidence and emerging clinical studies. Nevertheless, several obstacles should be overcome before the clinical translation of these approaches, such as using of standardized methods for modulating GM, identifying specific microbial signatures linked to various CNS illnesses, and understanding the exact mechanisms of gut-brain communication. This review provides a novel integrated perspective by comprehensively clarifying the bidirectional interactions between CNS pharmacological agents and microbiota-based therapeutic strategies in different neurological and psychiatric disorders, offering a unified framework to improve traditional pharmacological therapies. Importantly, future studies should concentrate on exploring the mechanisms and the exact interconnections between GM and CNS problems to elaborate targeted therapies for these disorders.

title: Epilepsy associated cognitive dysfunction and addiction: Possible mechanisms and clinical challenges.
abstract: Epilepsy is a complex neurological disorder that includes recurrent seizures and significant cognitive impairment, which substantially contribute to disease burden. This review presents an integrated mechanistic and clinical framework linking epilepsy, cognition, and addiction, emphasizing their shared and interacting neurobiological pathways. Recurrent seizure activity induces chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to disrupted synaptic plasticity and neurotransmitter imbalance, particularly within glutamatergic and dopaminergic systems. These alterations underlie deficits in memory, attention, and executive function. Concurrently, dysfunction of mesocorticolimbic reward circuitry increases susceptibility to substance use disorders, including alcohol, nicotine, opioid, and cannabis dependence. Substance use further destabilizes neuronal excitability, alters antiseizure drug pharmacokinetics, and accelerates cognitive decline, establishing a bidirectional and self-reinforcing cycle. Epigenetic modifications and maladaptive neuroplasticity further sustain this interaction. Clinically, the coexistence of epilepsy, cognitive impairment, and substance use presents major challenges, including diagnostic complexity, poor treatment adherence, polypharmacy, increased hospitalization, reduced functional independence, and elevated risk of mortality, including sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. These challenges highlight the limitations of seizure-focused care and the need for comprehensive management strategies. Moreover, therapeutic approaches should integrate cognitive rehabilitation, behavioral and psychological interventions, dietary therapies, neuromodulation techniques, and rational pharmacological optimization, alongside structured addiction management and supportive lifestyle measures. Multidisciplinary care models combining neurology, psychiatry, neuropsychology, and addiction medicine are essential for improving outcomes. Additionally, future directions should prioritize biomarker-driven precision medicine, longitudinal and standardized cognitive assessment, development of dual-targeted interventions, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory therapies, and the use of digital health technologies for monitoring and intervention. Early identification and integrated care remain critical to preventing long-term cognitive decline and addiction-related complications.

title: The Future of Chronic Disease and the Role of Governmental Public Health.
abstract: Chronic diseases have accounted for the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in the United States for decades. Today, the shape and context of chronic disease is changing. Therapeutic advances have transformed fatal conditions like HIV/AIDS and cancer into chronic conditions. Depression and Alzheimer disease are emerging as leading chronic conditions. Biomarkers are helping individuals determine their risk of certain cancers long before they appear, and technological devices like wearables, mobile applications, and self-administered tools are placing prevention in the hands of individuals. It is imperative that governmental public health redefine its role and look at new opportunities in primary prevention and early intervention of chronic disease. To assist the field, the authors offer recommendations and examples of health department-led initiatives that are meeting the moment in data and surveillance, education and communication, relationships with the health care and policy, environment, and systems efforts.

title: Role of APOE ɛ4 and ɛ2 With Longitudinal Cognitive Decline Among Those With Exceptional Longevity: The LifeAfter90 Study.
abstract:
APOE ɛ4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer disease, while ɛ2 is associated with decreased risk. However, it is unclear how these genotypes relate to cognitive decline among those aged older than 90+. We examined associations of ɛ4 and ɛ2 with longitudinal change in 3 cognitive domains among individuals aged 90+.
LifeAfter90 is an ongoing longitudinal multiethnic cohort study of those aged 90+. APOE genotyping was conducted using DNA extracted from saliva. Two dichotomous exposures were defined as ɛ4 carriers (ɛ2/ɛ4, ɛ3/ɛ4, or ɛ4/ɛ4 genotypes) vs non-ɛ4-carriers with no ɛ4 allele and ɛ2 carriers (ɛ2/2, ɛ2/3 genotypes) vs non-ɛ2-carriers (ɛ3/ɛ3, ɛ2/ɛ4, ɛ3/ɛ4, or ɛ4/ɛ4). Executive function (EF), semantic memory (SM), and verbal episodic memory (VEM) were measured every 6 months on up to 11 occasions using the Spanish and English Neuropsychological Scales. Time to all-cause mortality was calculated from baseline to death. We fit linear mixed-effects (LME) models and joint models (LME and Cox proportional hazard submodels) to account for the competing risk of death. Models adjusted for age and sex.
We evaluated 445 participants (mean age at baseline 93 years, SD 2.31, range 90-104; 59% female). In total, 20% were ɛ4 carriers, 15% were ɛ2 carriers, and 54% died during follow-up. The ethnoracial composition was 21% African American/Black, 22% as Asian, 16% as Hispanic/Latinx, 9% as multiracial/other, and 32% as White. The mean follow-up time was 3.9 years (SD 1.63, range 0.68-6.67). Neither ɛ4 nor ɛ2 carriers averaged substantially greater or lesser mortality hazard than noncarriers. In joint models, ɛ4 carriers had faster decline in EF (β = -0.07, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.02), but similar decline in VEM (β = -0.01, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.05) and SM (β = -0.03; 95% CI -0.08 to 0.02). APOE ɛ2 carriers had similar decline in EF (β = 0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.08) and SM (β = 0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.08) but slower decline in VEM (β = 0.07, 95% CI 0.00-0.15) compared with noncarriers. Longitudinal results were similar for LME and joint models.
After accounting for the competing risk of death, the negative consequences of ɛ4 on EF decline extend to those with exceptional longevity.

title: Akkermansia muciniphila gavage alleviates depression-like behaviors in female A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized not only by progressive motor deficits but also by non-motor symptoms, such as depression, which often emerge during the prodromal stage and significantly impair quality of life. While Akkermansia muciniphila (AKK) has shown potential in modulating neuroinflammation, its specific role and underlying mechanisms in alleviating PD-associated non-motor symptoms remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the effects of AKK intervention in 16-month-old female A53T α-synuclein (α-syn) transgenic mice. Behavioral assessments revealed that oral administration of AKK significantly ameliorated depression-like behaviors, evidenced by reduced immobility in the forced swim test and increased sucrose preference, without affecting motor function, spatial memory, or gastrointestinal motility. Mechanistically, the intervention exhibited genotype-specific effects: AKK significantly increased plasma 5-HT levels in C57 mice. This increase was associated with an enrichment of Lactobacillus taiwanensis and metabolic pathways favoring peripheral tryptophan conversion. Conversely, in A53T mice, the treatment specifically elevated hippocampal 5-HT levels without altering plasma concentrations. This central effect correlated with distinct microbial remodeling, characterized by the enrichment of butyrate/propionate-producing Lachnospiraceae and the activation of purine degradation. Collectively, these findings provide novel mechanistic insights into the therapeutic potential of AKK for managing non-motor symptoms in PD. While limited to a female cohort, our results suggest that AKK ameliorates depression-like behaviors in PD through sex-specific remodeling of the gut microbiome and serotonergic signaling.

title: Changes in modifiable dementia risk factors and subjective cognitive decline in mid and later life.
abstract:
Exposure to modifiable dementia risk factors (MDRFs) contributes substantially to dementia risk across the life course. Less is known about persistence and changes in these factors during mid- and later life and how they relate to early neurophysiological changes associated with dementia. This study examined rates and changes in MDRFs over two years and their associations with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) among older adults.
Cohort study.
Participants were 2370 adults aged 55-92 years (M = 68.54, SD = 7.15; 56.5% female) who completed the 2018 and 2020 waves of a longitudinal survey of ageing in New Zealand.
Self-reported hypertension, diabetes, hearing impairment, vision impairment, current smoking, hazardous alcohol use, physical inactivity, depression, and loneliness were classified into four categories across waves: stable absence, reduction, onset, and stable presence. SCD was assessed in 2020. Logistic regression models were used to examine associations between MDRF categories and SCD.
Survey-weighted responses indicated 8.6% of older adults experienced SCD. Diabetes, hearing impairment, current vision impairment, stable presence of physical inactivity, depression, and current loneliness were associated with increased odds of SCD.
Both the onset and reduction of psychosocial and sensory MDRFs in mid- and later life have measurable implications for subjective cognitive outcomes in a general population sample. Prevention and reduction of diabetes, sensory loss, physical inactivity, depression, and social isolation represent meaningful targets for supporting cognitive well-being among older adults.

title: A Frailty-integrated Prognostic Prediction Tool for Long-term Outcomes after Shunt Surgery in Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus: Development and Prospective Validation.
abstract: Long-term functional independence after shunt surgery for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus varies widely, particularly in older patients with multiple comorbidities. We aimed to develop and prospectively validate a frailty-integrated prognostic prediction tool to support patient selection and preoperative decision-making. A retrospective cohort of 82 patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus who underwent shunt surgery between 2005 and 2014 was used to develop a weighted idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus-specific frailty index based on multivariable logistic regression. The index incorporated neurological and non-neurological comorbidities, including dementia, cancer, depression, and movement disorders. The weighted idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus-specific frailty index was combined with preoperative modified Rankin Scale scores to estimate the probability of achieving functional independence (modified Rankin Scale ≤2) at 1, 2, and mid- to long-term follow-up (up to 4 years). Prospective validation was performed in an independent cohort of 30 patients treated between 2018 and 2023. The weighted idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus-specific frailty index demonstrated improved predictive performance, particularly for mid- to long-term outcomes (2-4 years), compared with conventional frailty indices, with higher correlation coefficients and lower Akaike Information Criterion values. Predicted probabilities of long-term independence declined stepwise with increasing frailty burden. In the validation cohort, predicted and observed outcomes showed good agreement, with adequate calibration confirmed by the Hosmer-Lemeshow test. This frailty-integrated prognostic prediction tool provides individualized estimates of long-term postoperative independence, particularly in the context of frailty and comorbidity burden. By incorporating comorbidity burden into preoperative assessment, the tool supports patient selection and shared decision-making and may facilitate realistic counseling and long-term care planning in older patients.

title: Self-Disclosure of HIV Status and the Relationship to Mental Health Among Adolescents Living With HIV in Uganda: A Cross-Sectional Secondary Analysis of a Longitudinal Cohort.
abstract: Research on self-disclosure of HIV status by adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) is scarce, despite its growing recognition as a determining factor of psychosocial outcomes and HIV treatment adherence, warranting examination of its mental health implications. A secondary analysis of longitudinal data of ALHIV in Uganda was conducted to assess patterns of self-disclosure and associations between sociodemographic factors, disclosure choices, and mental health symptoms. ALHIV disclosed to at least one person, most commonly a nuclear family member, with no significant associations except for disclosure to one's brother (i.e., lower depression symptoms). ALHIV who self-disclosed generally reported lower depression and anxiety symptoms, with a significant association observed for depression. The likelihood of ALHIV to disclose to family members highlights the importance of engaging these individuals in psychosocial interventions. Further research should clarify directionality and causality and examine the factors shaping ALHIV disclosure preferences to inform tailored care.

title: Seizures as a marker of severe multi-organ involvement in neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus: a diagnostic risk stratification study.
abstract:
This study aimed to identify independent predictors of seizure occurrence in patients with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE), develop a diagnostic model, and evaluate whether seizures are associated with adverse renal outcomes.
A retrospective cohort of 169 patients with NPSLE from Xiangya Hospital was analyzed. Among 70 pre-specified clinical, laboratory, and imaging variables, 20 variables associated with seizure occurrence (p < 0.05 in univariable logistic regression) were retained after multicollinearity screening (VIF < 5.0). Multivariable logistic regression was then performed to identify independent predictors of SE-NPSLE. Machine learning algorithms with fivefold cross-validation were then employed to develop and optimize the diagnostic model. Model performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC metrics. External validation was performed using an independent cohort (n = 46) from Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital. Renal survival rates were assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank tests.
Independent predictors of SE-NPSLE included anti-Rib-P antibody (OR = 0.315, 95% CI: 0.121-0.819), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (OR = 0.973 per mm/h, 95% CI: 0.954-0.992), and presence of psychosis (OR = 0.194, 95% CI: 0.057-0.659). A logistic regression-based nomogram (AUC: 0.818 training, 0.800 validation) demonstrated robust performance. External validation (n = 46) yielded an AUC of 0.706. What is more, NPSLE patients with seizures (SE-NPSLE) demonstrated significantly worse renal outcomes compared to NPSLE patients without seizures (non-SE-NPSLE).
Seizures in NPSLE are associated with poor renal prognosis. Our diagnostic model was developed to facilitate early risk assessment and may aid personalized seizure management; however, its clinical utility requires validation in larger, prospective cohorts. Key Points • A validated diagnostic model indentifies high-risk NPSLE patients for seizures. • 3 independent predictors of SE-NPSLE included anti-Rib-P antibodies, ESR and psychosis. • SE-NPSLE patients were youner, had higher SLEDAI, and exhibited more severe renal dysfunction than non-SE-NPSLE patients.

title: Zona incerta circuits in cognition and the regulation of sleep and wakefulness: potential relevance to Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline and prominent disturbances in sleep and wakefulness, reflecting dysfunction across distributed neural networks. The zona incerta (ZI) is a highly heterogeneous subthalamic structure whose organization is defined by spatial location, molecular identity, neurochemical phenotype, and circuit connectivity. Recent studies demonstrate that distinct ZI cell populations and projections contribute to memory processing, novelty seeking, cortical plasticity, sleep promotion, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, transitions to wakefulness, and sleep homeostasis. Together, these findings suggest that the ZI is better viewed as a state-dependent subcortical regulatory platform than as a unitary cognitive or sleep center. Emerging pathological evidence further raises the possibility that the ZI may be relevant to neurodegeneration. Amyloid-β deposition has been reported in the ZI of 5xFAD transgenic mice, while experimental tau propagation, human tauopathies other than AD, and studies of other neurodegenerative disorders indicate potential cellular and circuit vulnerability. However, direct evidence from human AD remains lacking, and no study has established a causal pathway from AD pathology to selective ZI dysfunction and subsequent cognitive or sleep impairment. We therefore propose two testable models in which the ZI contributes to AD phenotypes either as a shared circuit node or through parallel, selectively vulnerable functional modules.

title: zDHHC11 is a common palmitoyltransferase regulating microglia-mediated neuroinflammation across neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract:
Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation is a shared feature across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and diabetic cognitive impairment (DCI), but the convergent molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated whether protein S-palmitoylation serves as a common regulator of microglial neuroinflammation across distinct neurodegenerative diseases etiologies and aimed to identify the key palmitoyltransferase involved.
In vivo ND models (APP/PS1 for AD, MPTP for PD, STZ/high-fat diet for DCI) and in vitro BV2 microglial models stimulated with amyloid-β (Aβ), lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or high glucose (HG) were established. Microglial morphology, inflammatory responses, and the TLR4/MyD88 pathway were assessed by immunofluorescence, RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and ELISA. Protein palmitoylation levels were evaluated using 2-BP and ABE assays. Palmitoyltransferase expression profiling was performed, and protein-level validation was conducted both in vitro and in vivo. Subsequently, the identified common enzyme, zDHHC11, was knocked down by siRNA to determine its functional role.
All three ND models showed robust microglial activation with a pro-inflammatory amoeboid morphology. This upregulation was further corroborated at the protein level, with elevated zDHHC11 expression observed both in cultured cells and in brain tissue sections. Knockdown of Zdhhc11 suppressed cytokine expression/secretion and reduced TLR4/MyD88 levels, indicating that zDHHC11 acts upstream of this common pathway.
Protein S-palmitoylation mediated by zDHHC11 is a convergent mechanism driving microglial pro-inflammatory activation across distinct ND etiologies. zDHHC11 represents a common regulator of TLR4/MyD88-dependent neuroinflammation and a potential therapeutic target for multiple NDs.

title: Hemi-see-saw nystagmus with superimposed pendular oculopalatal tremor: case report and systematic review.
abstract:
Hemi-see-saw nystagmus (HSSN) is an uncommon subtype, characterized by elevation and intorsion of one eye with contralateral depression and extorsion, typically in a jerk pattern. It is associated with unilateral lesions of the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and the medial longitudinal fasciculus, both of which are involved in the ocular tilt reaction (OTR). Although its association with oculopalatal tremor (OPT) has been described, it is rare.
We performed a systematic review of seven databases on HSSN, extracting data on demographics, etiology, lesion location, oculomotor findings, nystagmus pattern, outcomes, and in addition we presented a representative case.
A systematic review of seven databases identified 18 reports comprising 57 cases of HSSN or closely related dissociated vertical-torsional nystagmus, including the present index case. The mean age was 56.2 ± 16.3 years, and 63.2% of patients were male. Ischemic stroke was the most frequent etiology (75.4%), followed by hemorrhagic stroke (14.0%). Less frequent causes included Chiari I malformation, demyelinating/inflammatory disease, cavernous malformation, ataxia with oculomotor apraxia type 2, Joubert syndrome, and brainstem encephalitis (1.8% each). Jerk nystagmus predominated (82.5%), whereas pendular nystagmus was identified in 17.5%, exclusively in the setting of OPT or inferior olivary hypertrophy. Among jerk HSSN cases, the pontine tegmentum was the most frequent lesion site (63.8%), with INO present in all pontine cases and OTR in 90.0%. Complete resolution was reported predominantly in cases associated with INO, whereas lack of improvement was confined to OPT-related cases, with one exception of spontaneous resolution after 20 years. We describe a 30-year-old man with a pontomedullary arteriovenous malformation presenting with pendular HSSN, right one-and-a-half syndrome, gaze-evoked nystagmus, OTR, incomplete Horner syndrome, and OPT.
HSSN is an uncommon nystagmus, most often vascular in origin and frequently involving the pontine tegmentum. While it usually presents with a jerk waveform, association with OPT may produce a pendular phenotype, suggesting a distinct brainstem-cerebellar mechanism. Larger anatomically and oculographically characterized series are needed to clarify structure-function correlations and prognosis.

title: Improving the fairness and robustness of deep learning classification models through bias mitigation and post hoc calibration.
abstract:
The goal of this study was to enhance the fairness and clinical applicability of deep learning models for classifying Alzheimer's disease from structural MRI scans. To achieve this, we addressed two key challenges: age-related bias and unreliable probability estimates. Specifically, we investigated in-processing debiasing strategies to achieve age-invariant predictions while preserving diagnostic accuracy. We also systematically evaluated post hoc calibration methods to improve the reliability, interpretability, and clinical usefulness of predicted probabilities across diverse patient populations.
Structural MRI data from three independent cohorts (ADNI, AIBL, and DELCODE) were preprocessed using a standardized pipeline. Age-related bias was addressed using two in-processing strategies, adversarial training (CF-Net) and GLM-based feature residualization (PMDN), implemented in a shared 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) framework. Additionally, post hoc calibration was performed using four regression methods: logistic, probit, isotonic, and Bayesian binning. We evaluated model performance, fairness, and calibration using classification as well as calibration-specific metrics.
PMDN achieved the best overall performance, with higher balanced accuracy (0.71) and improved calibration (Brier ≈ 0.22), showing substantially reduced variability compared to baseline and CF-Net. PMDN effectively removed age-related bias, achieving near-zero age prediction correlation; CF-Net, however, showed only partial and unstable debiasing. Post hoc calibration further improved probability reliability, with nonparametric methods (isotonic regression and Bayesian binning) yielding the lowest calibration errors (MCE ≈ 0.21-0.24).
This study shows that, although deep learning models achieve similar classification performance, they differ significantly in terms of calibration, stability, and fairness. PMDN provides more consistent and effective age bias mitigation than the CF-Net approach, particularly in clinically relevant subgroups. Post hoc calibration improves probability reliability further, with nonparametric methods achieving the best calibration.

title: A genome-wide association study of cognitive impairment in a Chinese cohort of 1,040 individuals.
abstract: While genetic heritability plays a major role in the development of cognitive impairment, most genetic risk factors are identified from studies of European populations. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on cognitive impairment in the Chinese population by sequencing 1,040 matched case-control individuals from a longitudinal cohort of Zhejiang Province, China. We detected 19 SNPs clustered in 15 genomic loci reaching suggestive significance (P < 1 × 10- 5). Eleven of these genomic loci are newly associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) or cognitive impairment, among which five (GRP39, FAT1, EDIL3, ZNF596, and PDGFD) show nominal evidence of replication in both external GWAS of AD in East-Asian populations and summary statistics of AD in diverse populations. The detected loci are implicated in micronutrient homeostasis including zinc (GPR39), iron (STEAP1), potassium (KCNJ6), and vitamin K (VKORC1L1), cell connections (EVPLL) through cadherin regulations (PCDH18, FAT1), regulating amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP) (EDIL3), formation of amyloid-β (EDEM1) and neurofibrillary tangles (PDGFD, ZNF596), neuronal growth (NEGR1), and phosphatase regulations (SETBP1, TPTE). This study presents a robust GWAS for cognitive impairment in the Chinese population and highlights a promising set of therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative disorder.

title: Early disruptions in brain capillary blood flow control in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: In Alzheimer's disease (AD), vascular dysfunction and impaired control of brain blood flow can disrupt cellular bioenergetics decades before cognitive decline. Identifying the earliest vascular changes is therefore critical for developing therapies that intervene before the cascading events leading to neuronal decline. Brain energy supply is dynamically controlled by the cerebral vasculature, where capillary thin-strand pericytes are emerging as key players. We recently identified a central role for ATP-sensitive potassium (K+, KATP) channels in enabling thin-strand pericytes to sense local neuronal activity and generate hyperpolarizing signals that are transmitted via capillary endothelial cells to upstream arterioles, eliciting increases in blood flow. Importantly, thin-strand pericyte KATP channels are the centerpiece of an electro-metabolic "energy switch" mechanism that couples decreases in local glucose to hyperemia, providing a failsafe to ensure continual energy substrate supply to support neuronal function. Disruption of this mechanism could therefore precipitate an imbalance between demand and supply, creating an energy gap for neurons that leads to deleterious consequences. We demonstrate that capillary control of blood flow is disrupted in the early stages of disease progression in mice expressing familial AD mutations (5xFAD). Transgenic 5xFAD mice exhibit early disruption of capillary signaling, beginning with dysfunctional endothelial inward rectifier K+ (Kir)2.1 channels at 2-4 mo, disabling transmission of KATP-mediated signals to upstream blood flow control machinery, followed by direct impairment of pericyte KATP channel function by 6-8 mo. Together, these deficits cause early and sustained failure of electrical signaling from deep capillary pericytes to upstream arterioles and arteriole-capillary transition (ACT) zone vessels, limiting KATP-dependent energy-switch-mediated blood flow control. Our findings define a temporal and mechanistic framework linking familial AD mutations to early capillary signaling dysfunction and highlight preservation of capillary blood flow control as a potential therapeutic target to protect against downstream effects of amyloid β accumulation.

title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Pharmacological evidence suggesting the involvement of autophagy-related signaling in the cognitive effects of neuropeptide Y in an amyloid-β-induced model of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract:
Neuropeptide Y (NPY) exerts neuroprotective effects; however, its functional relationship with autophagy-related signaling pathways in AD-associated cognitive dysfunction remains insufficiently understood. Using an Aβ-induced rat model of AD, the present study evaluated the effects of NPY on learning and memory. Specifically, we examined whether pharmacological manipulation with 3-methyladenine and MHY1485 modifies the cognitive effects of NPY, providing an indirect behavioral-pharmacological assessment of processes potentially related to autophagy and mTOR signaling.
This experimental study was conducted on 88 male Wistar rats (200-250 g) randomly divided to 11 groups (n = 8 per group). An intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection of Aβ (2 µg/µl per rat) was used to induce the AD model. NPY (10 ng /µl), MHY1485 (an mTOR activator; 2 µM), and 3-methyladenine (3-MA; an autophagy inhibitor; 300 nmol, 30 nmol, and 3 µmol) were administered via ICV injection. Cognitive performance was assessed using the passive avoidance and Y-maze tasks.
NPY administration significantly decreased time spent in the dark compartment (TDC), increased step-through latency (STL) in the passive avoidance task, and enhanced spontaneous alternation behavior in the Y-maze (P < 0.05). Importantly, administration of MHY1485 and 3-MA (300 nM), either alone or in combination, significantly attenuated the cognitive-enhancing effects of NPY (P < 0.05) CONCLUSION: NPY improved cognitive performance in an Aβ-induced rat model of Alzheimer's disease. Our behavioral-pharmacological findings suggest that autophagy-related signaling contributes to the memory-enhancing effects of NPY. Pharmacological modulation with 3-MA and MHY1485 provides functional evidence consistent with the potential involvement of Beclin-1- and mTOR-related signaling, although direct molecular confirmation warrants further investigation.

title: Cryo-EM advances in TDP-43 amyloid fibrils structure determination.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a DNA/RNA-binding protein whose pathological aggregation characterizes a spectrum of neurodegenerative disorders known as TDP-43 proteinopathies, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Recent breakthroughs in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have revolutionized our understanding of these diseases by resolving the atomic structures of TDP-43 amyloid fibrils. These structural insights have been pivotal in elucidating the transition from functional liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to irreversible solid-state aggregation. This review synthesizes key cryo-EM findings from 2019 to 2026, encompassing fibrils formed by the full-length low-complexity domain, disease-relevant core fragments, and filaments extracted directly from patient tissues, as well as the pathological implications of distinct structural polymorphs. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the brain science aspects of the pathogenesis of TDP-43 proteinopathies, but also provide an important structural basis for the development of specific conformational diagnostic methods and targeted therapeutic drugs.

title: Potential Mechanisms of N-Methyltyramine in Multitarget Regulation of Mental Disorders via the GPCR-cAMP Pathway.
abstract: N-Methyltyramine (NMT) is a tyramine derivative widely distributed in citrus plants and the traditional Chinese medicine Zhishi. Pharmacological studies have confirmed that NMT directly binds to the dopamine D₂ receptor (DRD2; Ki = 31.3µM), inhibits forskolin-induced cAMP accumulation (EC₅₀ ≈ 4µM, Emax = 89%), and dose-dependently antagonizes quinpirole-mediated β-arrestin2 recruitment, exhibiting G protein-biased agonistic properties. Meanwhile, NMT activates the human trace amine-associated receptor 1 (hTAAR1; EC₅₀ ≈ 2µM) to increase cAMP, possesses α₂-adrenergic receptor antagonistic activity (IC₅₀ = 5.53µM), and exhibits blood-brain barrier permeability (logPe = -5.16cm/s). Based on these multi-target receptor profiles, NMT may participate in the regulation of central monoaminergic neurotransmission via the GPCR-cAMP signaling axis, providing a new multi-target lead compound direction for research on neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, depression, and drug addiction. Notably, evidence for direct activation of β₂-adrenergic receptors by NMT remains insufficient, and its therapeutic effects and downstream signal integration mechanisms require NMT-specific experimental validation.

title: A multimodal MRI-based study of early-stage Parkinson's disease across age-at-onset groups.
abstract:
This study aimed to investigate distinct iron deposition and neurite microstructural alterations in deep gray matter nuclei between early-onset Parkinson's disease (EOPD) and late-onset Parkinson's disease (LOPD) patients using quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI), and to evaluate the ability of these quantitative metrics to distinguish EOPD and LOPD from their corresponding healthy controls.
Fifty-three early-stage PD patients (15 EOPD and 38 LOPD) and 58 healthy controls (17 young healthy controls and 41 older healthy controls) underwent multimodal MRI. QSM-derived magnetic susceptibility and NODDI-derived parameters (NDI, Viso, ODI) were analyzed in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), red nucleus (RN), globus pallidus (GP), putamen (PT), and caudate nucleus (CN).
In EOPD, the iron content in deep gray matter nuclei was not significantly different from that in young healthy controls, but ODI was reduced in the left SNc. In LOPD, increased QSM values were observed in bilateral SNc, PT, and left CN, alongside decreased NDI and increased Viso in the left SNc, and reduced ODI in bilateral SNc and PT. Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that the combination of the NDI and ODI in the left SNc could effectively differentiate patients with EOPD from young healthy controls, whereas the optimal combination for distinguishing patients with LOPD from older healthy controls consisted of the NDI, ODI, and QSM in the left SNc.
Multimodal MRI revealed distinct spatial involvement patterns in early-stage EOPD and LOPD and showed potential for distinguishing PD patients from their corresponding healthy controls.

title: Habitual Diet, Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis, and α-Synucleinopathy Conversion in Isolated Rapid Eye Movement (REM) Sleep Behavior Disorder.
abstract:
Accumulating evidence indicates that habitual diet, including plant-based dietary patterns, is associated with neurodegenerative α-synucleinopathy risk. However, the role of diet and its correlation with the gut microbiome in prodromal α-synucleinopathy, specifically among patients with isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), remains unclear.
To evaluate dietary patterns, their interplay with gut microbial dysbiosis, and longitudinal effects on neurodegenerative progression in iRBD patients.
We recruited 287 iRBD patients and 208 age- and sex-matched controls. Plant-based diet indices (PDIs) were derived from food frequency questionnaires. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed in 456 subjects for diet-microbiome analyses. After a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 45 (15.7%) iRBD patients converted to α-synucleinopathies. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the associations between diet and neurodegenerative outcomes.
We found that iRBD patients exhibited lower healthful PDIs (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.48 [0.29-0.80], P = 0.005) but higher consumption of unhealthful plant-based foods (refined grains, sweets, and sweeteners). Diet-microbiome interaction analysis identified dietary associations for 84.3% of iRBD-related gut microbes, including co-occurrence between healthful PDI and Clostridium sp. AF20-17LB. Longitudinally, four dietary factors and five iRBD-related microbes were associated with neurodegenerative outcomes; specifically, higher coffee consumption was linked to a lower risk of progression to α-synucleinopathy (aHR [95% CI]: 0.30 [0.11-0.78], P = 0.01). Furthermore, mediation analyses indicated that the iRBD-enriched species Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans mediated the association between unhealthful PDI and dementia-first conversion.
Habitual diet in iRBD is associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis and predicts neurodegenerative progression. These findings highlight diet-microbiome interactions as modifiable targets for intervention in prodromal α-synucleinopathy. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Concurrent diagnostic efficiency and 8-year measurement stability of the weighted subjective memory complaints questionnaire-revised.
abstract: BackgroundSubjective memory complaints (SMC) are a potential early indicator of dementia, but whether their measurement properties hold over years of repeated assessment is unexamined. The weighted Subjective Memory Complaints Questionnaire-Revised (SMCQ-R) showed higher cross-sectional accuracy than the original SMCQ, but its performance over extended follow-up requires verification.ObjectiveTo evaluate whether SMCQ-R maintains measurement fidelity over 8 years relative to SMCQ and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE).MethodsWe analyzed 2057 community-dwelling older adults without baseline major depressive disorder from the Korean Longitudinal Study on Cognitive Aging and Dementia (KLOSCAD), followed biennially for 8 years (5 assessments). Concurrent discriminative performance was evaluated via AUC, Cohen's d, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Sensitivity analysis excluded participants with incident depression during follow-up, and separately used all available data.ResultsAll three measures demonstrated excellent cross-sectional validity (mean AUC: SMCQ-R = 0.883, SMCQ = 0.889, MMSE = 0.884). SMCQ-R showed numerically larger effect sizes than SMCQ (Cohen's |d|: 1.884 versus 1.742, p = 0.154) and higher SNR (1.659 versus 1.485, p = 0.327), neither significant. Both subjective measures showed significant SNR reductions with incident depression, whereas MMSE remained robust.ConclusionsSMCQ-R showed a significant AUC decline over 8 years (slope = -0.0079/year, p = 0.024), but maintained clinically adequate accuracy (AUC ≥ 0.844), similar to SMCQ (0.883 vresus 0.889), despite a 36% reduction in item burden. SMCQ-R is regarded as an efficient complement to the MMSE rather than evidence of its superiority.

title: An updated patent review of mGlu5 negative allosteric modulators (2018 - present).
abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor subtype 5 (mGlu5) is an important regulator of excitatory neurotransmission and remains a therapeutic target for neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders, including substance use disorders, depression, Fragile X syndrome, Parkinson's disease-related dyskinesia, and other movement disorders. However, the clinical development of mGlu5 negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) has been limited by translational challenges, inconsistent efficacy, and safety concerns, particularly hepatotoxicity associated with early acetylene-containing scaffolds such as ADX10059. The study provides an updated assessment of the mGlu5 NAM patent landscape and related medicinal chemistry advances from 2018 to the present. The post-2018 period is characterised as a phase of translational and medicinal chemistry refinement, marked by a shift from metabolically unstable aryl-alkyne and acetylene-based chemotypes towards more stable heterocyclic, bicyclic, and non-acetylene frameworks. Key strategies include scaffold hopping, structure-based drug design, receptor occupancy assessment, and pharmacokinetic optimisation to reduce the risk of bioactivation, improve brain exposure, and enhance clinical translatability. Recent patent-linked compounds such as TMP-301/HTL0014242, VU0424238, VU6031545, VU6024945, and AE90015 are presented alongside unconventional approaches, including GET-73, LCGM-10, antibodies, and nanobodies. It also covers clinical progress, including the repurposing of mavoglurant/STP7 for cocaine use disorder. Overall, the field aims for safer, more selective, and better-controlled mGlu5 modulation strategies, but challenges related to efficacy, tolerability, and patient selection continue to hinder clinical success.

title: Chronic lead exposure disrupts copper redox homeostasis and aggravates neurodegeneration.
abstract: Lead (Pb) represents a critical environmental health concern due to its profound impact on neurodegenerative processes. However, its specific influence on copper (Cu) redox states and the associated neurotoxic mechanisms remain inadequately understood. In this study, male wild-type C57BL/6 and 5xFAD Alzheimer's disease (AD) model mice were used to investigate how chronic low-dose Pb exposure (200 μg/L via drinking water) exacerbated AD-related pathology through perturbation of Cu homeostasis. Elemental analysis revealed that Pb exposure depleted essential cerebral metals, including Ca, Mg, Fe, and Zn. In contrast to these metals, Cu showed concurrent accumulation in both the brain and bloodstream, particularly in the ADPb group, consistent with disturbed Cu homeostasis in the AD background. In situ fluorescent imaging demonstrated that Pb exposure significantly disrupted the Cu(I)/Cu(II) valence balance within the hippocampus. While the unexposed AD brain showed relatively higher Cu(I) signals, Pb exposure shifted the fluorescence pattern toward Cu(II). Behavioral assessments further indicated that Pb exposure was associated with reduced locomotor activity, anxiety-like responses, and accelerated spatial memory decay in AD mice. Histopathological and immunofluorescence evaluations structurally confirmed these functional deficits, revealing disorganized hippocampal cytoarchitecture, myelin loss, and accelerated Aβ plaque deposition in the ADPb group. Ultimately, these findings demonstrated that environmental Pb exacerbated AD progression not solely through direct physical toxicity, but fundamentally by disrupting the in situ Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox equilibrium. This study highlights Cu redox imbalance as a potential mediator linking Pb exposure with AD progression and warrants further biochemical validation.

title: Global cognitive and verbal episodic memory impairment in the post-acute phase of anti-nmdar encephalitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis with narrative synthesis.
abstract:
Cognitive impairment is a recognized long-term complication of anti-NMDAR encephalitis, but its pooled magnitude, domain specificity, and time course have not been systematically quantified.
To quantify pooled global cognitive and verbal episodic memory impairment in convalescent anti-NMDAR encephalitis relative to healthy comparators, and to assess whether impairment magnitude changes with time since disease onset.
We systematically reviewed observational studies assessing standardized cognitive outcomes in adults with cell-based-assay-confirmed anti-NMDAR encephalitis during the post-acute/convalescent phase. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL were searched from inception to 20 June 2026. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed for cognitive domains with at least three independent cohorts, while other domains were synthesized narratively according to SWiM principles.
Fourteen independent cohorts comprising 439 patients were included. Six cohorts (191 patients, 182 controls) contributed to the confirmed primary global-cognition analysis, showing substantial impairment (Hedges' g - 1.26, 95% CI - 1.49 to - 1.04; I²=0%). Verbal episodic memory was also impaired (g - 0.88, 95% CI - 1.13 to - 0.63; 5 cohorts). Recognition was impaired alongside recall in the two cohorts reporting recognition trials. Narrative synthesis identified frequent executive and working-memory impairment, impaired speeded processing, and deficits in visual episodic memory and language, whereas visuospatial findings were less consistent.
Post-acute anti-NMDAR encephalitis is associated with substantial global cognitive and verbal episodic memory impairment, with additional deficits across several cognitive domains. Comprehensive longitudinal neuropsychological assessment, including social cognition and psychiatric symptoms, is needed to clarify recovery trajectories and mechanisms.

title: Positioning Cenobamate in the Treatment Algorithm of Focal Epilepsy: Seizure Control and Benefits Beyond Seizures.
abstract: This work integrates the opinion on the current use of cenobamate (CNB) of an expert panel structured across seven thematic domains: efficacy, patient profiles, titration and dosing, pharmacokinetic interactions, safety, parallel effects, and therapeutic positioning. According to personal experience and scientific evidence, experts unanimously regarded CNB as likely more efficacious than other newer-generation antiseizure medications (ASMs), particularly based on the long-term sustained seizure-freedom rates, despite the absence of comparative head-to-head studies. Priority candidates are patients with focal epilepsy failing two or more ASMs, including older patients, with a clear inclination toward earlier introduction. Initial response is expected at 100-200 mg/day, although maintenance is typically 200 mg/day or higher, alongside reduction of concomitant ASMs particularly sodium channel blockers and benzodiazepines. The most relevant drug-drug interaction is with clobazam, which may have a synergistic efficacy effect and in parallel increases plasma concentrations of clobazam, thereby inducing adverse events. The most frequent adverse events (somnolence, dizziness, fatigue) are dose-dependent and are reduced by anticipatory reduction of concomitant medication. Beyond seizure reduction, an early intervention with CNB may modify the prognosis of epilepsy, reducing the long-term mortality risk, cognitive impairment, or psychiatric disorders. The panel converged on a priority to position CNB as a third-line treatment in the focal epilepsy treatment algorithm owing to its high efficacy, which will probably lead to modification of the long-term global outcomes of people with epilepsy.

title: Profile of migrant people with non-medically supervised use of pregabalin: a scoping review.
abstract:
Pregabalin is a gabapentinoid drug used to treat neuropathic pain, epilepsy and anxiety. Over recent years, prescriptions and non-medically supervised use of pregabalin have increased in several European countries, especially within the French-speaking regions. These increases have been reported in young migrants, particularly those from Maghreb. However, the available peer-reviewed literature is poor with respect to the main characteristics of migrant people with non-medically supervised use of pregabalin and their trajectory of use. This scoping review explored both indexed scientific databases and grey literature to better identify the profile of pregabalin users, including their geographical origin, context and motivations of use, sociodemographic and psychiatric features.
A search of relevant articles was conducted in several scientific databases of peer-reviewed journals, complemented by grey literature retrieved from reference lists of peer-reviewed publications and interviews with professionals involved in migrant support and healthcare.
Two main populations of migrants using non-medically supervised pregabalin were identified. The first and main group consists of people coming from Maghreb, primarily from Algeria. They are commonly young socially marginalized men, who use pregabalin to experience euphoria or to cope with psychological trauma. These individuals usually migrate for economic reasons, and they frequently seek to specifically migrate to French-speaking countries for linguistic or family reasons. Pregabalin initiation is generally reported in the country of origin, and continues post-migration, in the context of precarious living situations or enrollment in criminal networks that provide an easier access to the drug, in exchange for engaging in different illicit activities. The second identified population with non-medically supervised use of pregabalin comes from Eastern Europe, and consists of older male individuals, who usually report using pregabalin to enhance or replace opioid drugs. In this second group, migration is motivated by economic or political reasons, and/or for getting access to healthcare services for chronic viral infections, such as Human Immunodeficiency Virus or Hepatitis B or C virus. They do not specifically aim to migrate into a French-speaking country.
The increase in non-medically supervised use of pregabalin observed among migrant people in many Western European countries seems to be mainly related to two distinct migrant populations, i.e., Maghreb, and Eastern European respectively. Between the two categories of migrant people, motivations for pregabalin use, as well as migration trajectories, seem to be different, suggesting that prevention, harm-reduction and treatment strategies should be tailored to each group.

title: Device-Associated Sepsis and Brain Injury: Transitioning From Early Infection Control to Late Neuroprotection.
abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a complex neuroinflammatory condition characterized by diffuse brain dysfunction arising from systemic infection without direct central nervous system invasion. In modern critical care, device-associated infections (DAIs) caused by invasive medical devices, such as central line-associated bloodstream infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and catheter-associated urinary tract infections, have become critical drivers of intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired sepsis. Biofilm formation on these devices establishes persistent inflammatory reservoirs that continuously shed microorganisms, pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) into the circulation, sustaining systemic immune activation. This review outlines an integrated mechanistic framework linking DAIs to acute brain dysfunction. Systemic inflammation and endothelial activation trigger microvascular dysfunction, impaired cerebral autoregulation, and blood-brain barrier disruption. These peripheral vascular alterations allow inflammatory mediators to access the central nervous system, where they induce microglial and astrocytic reactivity. Persistent neuroimmune activation compromises neurotransmitter homeostasis-causing glutamate excitotoxicity and cholinergic deficits-while impairing neuronal mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. The resulting oxidative stress, energy failure, and self-amplifying neuroinflammatory feedback loops culminate in synaptic damage and neuronal injury. Clinically, this manifests as altered consciousness, delirium, seizures, and long-term neurocognitive impairment. By framing SAE as a concurrent, multidimensional continuum rather than a linear sequence, this review highlights the critical role of early infection prevention, timely device removal, and targeted neuroprotective strategies aimed at stabilizing vascular integrity and mitigating neuroinflammation.

title: Video EEG in pediatric epilepsy: Diagnostic significance and association between frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity.
abstract:
This study aimed to compare video electroencephalogram (VEEG) and routine electroencephalogram (EEG) in childhood epilepsy diagnosis and analyze the correlation between EEG frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity.
One hundred and sixty children suspected of having epilepsy underwent routine EEG and VEEG examinations. Diagnostic efficacy and detection rates were compared. Cognitive function was evaluated in 80 children diagnosed with epilepsy, who were allocated into normal intelligence (35 cases), borderline intelligence (25 cases), and intelligence-impaired (20 cases) groups. Clinical data, EEG parameters, and their correlation with cognitive impairment were analyzed.
VEEG showed higher sensitivity, accuracy, and negative predictive value, and detection rates of epileptiform discharges, synchronous clinical seizures, and clinical symptoms than routine EEG (p < 0.05). Clinical characteristics and EEG parameters differed among the three groups (p < 0.05). The relative power of δ and θ bands and the awake and sleep discharge indices were positively correlated with cognitive impairment severity (r = 0.300, 0.643, 0.622, and 0.456), whereas α and β band power were negatively correlated (r = -0.515 and -0.410) (all p < 0.001).
VEEG demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than routine EEG, and EEG frequency band power was correlated with cognitive impairment severity.

title: Is it safe-and ethical-to prescribe THC to youth?
abstract: The medical use of cannabis-derived products in children and adolescents has expanded beyond established indications for purified cannabidiol (CBD), with increasing investigation of CBD-rich extracts containing Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) for neuropsychiatric conditions. Although preliminary studies suggest potential symptomatic benefits, the evidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous formulations, short follow-up, and insufficient assessment of long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Unlike CBD, THC directly activates CB1 receptors as a partial agonist, a pharmacological property underlying both its therapeutic and psychoactive effects. Following oral administration, THC undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism to the psychoactive metabolite 11-hydroxy-THC, with substantial interindividual variability in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics supporting individualized dosing according to clinical response and tolerability. Experimental studies raise concerns regarding THC exposure during neurodevelopment, while observational studies associate frequent, high-potency recreational cannabis use with cognitive impairment, psychosis, and other adverse psychiatric outcomes. These findings cannot be directly extrapolated to regulated medicinal cannabinoid use, which differs substantially in product composition, dosing, administration, therapeutic indication, and clinical monitoring. Nevertheless, long-term neurodevelopmental safety data for medicinal THC exposure in children and adolescents remain limited. These uncertainties must be weighed against the consequences of inadequately treated disease, particularly severe drug-resistant epilepsy. Accordingly, the risk-benefit assessment of THC-containing products should be individualized, considering disease severity, treatment refractoriness, available evidence-based alternatives, therapeutic response, and tolerability. Long-term prospective studies and improved patient-selection strategies are needed to better define the role of THC-containing medicinal products in pediatric populations.

title: Psychoneuroimmunology of glioblastoma: How emotional states shape tumor biology.
abstract: Psychological states profoundly influence physiological processes, with growing evidence linking emotional dysregulation to cancer progression. Within the framework of psychoneuroimmunology, recent findings have shown that chronic stress, depression and anxiety disrupt immune surveillance and promote a pro-inflammatory environment that favors tumor growth. Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), the most aggressive brain tumor, appears particularly sensitive to these neuroimmune influences. Some stress mediators and neurotransmitters-such as glucocorticoids and catecholamines- modulate the GBM microenvironment, fostering tumor-supportive pathways and epigenetic changes. This comprehensive review synthesizes evidence connecting emotional disturbances and glioma biology, highlighting shared neuroimmune mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities. We propose that integrating psychosocial and neuropharmacological strategies into GBM care could improve patients outcomes by targeting both tumor biology and emotional well-being.

title: D2 dopamine and CB2 cannabinoid receptor cooperation restores striatal LTP in an epilepsy model.
abstract: Increasing evidence suggests that subcortical structures contribute to seizure susceptibility and cognitive impairment in several epileptic syndromes. However, research into mechanisms linking neuronal excitability and synaptic dysfunction in epilepsy has mainly focused on the cortex and hippocampus, leaving basal ganglia contributions largely unexplored. Using a genetic murine model of Lafora disease (LD), a drug-resistant form of neurodegenerative epilepsy, we performed ex vivo patch-clamp recordings to assess neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, and plasticity of striatal medium spiny neurons. Our results reveal progressive alterations in corticostriatal transmission and long-term synaptic plasticity, including long-term potentiation (LTP). Electrophysiological and biochemical assessments showed a reduced NMDA/AMPA ratio and reduced expression of NMDA receptor subunits and dopamine receptors in striatal neurons of LD mice. Exposure to a dopamine D2 receptor agonist and to cannabidiol restored long-term plasticity in LD mice, suggesting a D2R- and CB2R-dependent synergic action on striatal LTP. Our findings highlight basal ganglia dysfunction in experimental epilepsy and suggest an unconventional dopaminergic-endocannabinoid interplay.

title: Unmet needs for opioid agonist therapy in Iranian prisons: a cross-sectional study.
abstract:
This study aims to estimate the prevalence of inadequate opioid agonist therapy (OAT) uptake and explore associated factors among people who use nonmedical opioids inside prisons in Iran.
Using data from a national bio-behavioral surveillance survey, the authors conducted a multi-stage random sampling of 5,785 people in prison in 33 major prisons. Of these, 2994 (51.8%) participants with regular (i.e. at least weekly) nonmedical opioid use in the past month before entering prison or in the previous month inside the prison or prior OAT access before or during incarceration were eligible. The authors built multivariable logistic regression models to assess factors associated with limited OAT uptake inside prisons, reporting adjusted odds ratio (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).
Participants averaged 36.1 years (SD: 8.6); 97.2% were male. Overall, 32.5% (95% CI: 30.8%, 34.2%) of eligible participants for receiving OAT inside prison, had no OAT uptake. Of those previously on OAT, 40.8% discontinued treatment after incarceration. Factors associated with no OAT uptake included: age ≤ 30 (aOR = 1.74; 95% CI: 1.47, 2.07), recent prison drug use (aOR = 1.56; 95% CI: 1.29, 1.88), insufficient HIV knowledge (aOR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.32, 2.11). Protective factors included lifetime injection drug use history (aOR = 0.43; 95% CI: 0.34, 0.55), HIV testing history (aOR = 0.78; 95% CI: 0.66, 0.92) and current depression/anxiety (aOR = 0.61; 95% CI: 0.52, 0.72).
Despite OAT availability in Iranian prisons, one-third of eligible participants did not access treatment. Prior harm reduction engagement was consistently associated with uptake, supporting the need for systematic screening at prison entry, strengthened community-to-prison care continuity and integrated mental health services.

title: Escherichia coli hns and methylglyoxal link gut microbial metabolism to host neuronal gene regulation in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra (SN). Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in PD pathogenesis, how defined bacterial genes and their metabolites influence host neuronal gene regulation remains unclear. Here, we identify a gut microbial hns-methylglyoxal (MG) pathway linking Escherichia coli (E. coli) metabolism to host neuronal gene regulation. In the stool metagenomic cohort, hns, a bacterial gene encoding the histone-like nucleoid structuring protein and primarily derived from E. coli, was enriched particularly in body-first PD, a subtype associated with gut-originating pathology. In a separate plasma MG cohort, plasma levels of MG, a reactive metabolite whose bacterial production was hns-dependent in our model system, were higher in body-first than in brain-first PD and were nominally inversely associated with cardiac meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) uptake within the body-first group. Using Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) PD models, we found that feeding with Δhns E. coli protected dopaminergic neurons, whereas exogenous MG abolished this neuroprotection. Transcriptomic and neuronal RNAi analyses identified rig-5 as a host mediator of hns deletion-induced neuroprotection. Cross-species analyses identified LSAMP as a candidate mammalian ortholog of rig-5. MG suppressed LSAMP expression in human neuronal cells, and LSAMP expression was reduced in the post-mortem SN of patients with PD. Conversely, Lsamp expression was increased in the SN of mice colonized with Δhns E. coli. Together, these findings delineate a microbial gene-metabolite-host gene pathway through which E. coli hns and MG modulate rig-5-dependent dopaminergic vulnerability in C. elegans, with corresponding changes of LSAMP expression in mammalian systems.

title: Network pharmacology-driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed for 128 active targets by STRING database and Cytoscape software. Further, active target-associated pathways analysed using ClueGO plugin Cytoscape software and the Reactome online public domain server. The non-competitive allosteric PTP1B inhibition through the design of Simufilam derivatives, with particular emphasis on A20, which is predicted to bind at the non-competitive allosteric site of the PTP1B protein (PDB ID: 1T49), involves α3, α6, and α7 helices that influence the WPD loop orientation. The proposed non-competitive allosteric binding mode is based on computational evidence and for that further experimental validation would be required to conclusively confirm binding of the designed compounds within this regulatory region. Using in-silico approaches, including molecular docking, identified A20 with the most favourable predicted binding energy score (-10.8 kcal/mol) compared to other derivatives. Molecular dynamics simulations further indicated structural stability of the PTP1B-A20, 26, and co-crystal complex, with consistent RMSD, RMSF, H-bond, Rg, and SASA. Principal component analysis suggested that A20 restricts conformational flexibility; hence MM-PBSA analysis displayed its stable binding free energies. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation characterized the polarity, stability, and reactivity of A20 studies supported its favourable electronic configuration. Overall, A20 displayed superior calculated binding energies, trajectory stability, and predicted drug-likeness, positioning it as a promising lead candidate for future empirical validation in AD research.

title: Familial Darier Disease Across 3 Generations: Highlighting the Spectrum of Neuropsychiatric Comorbidities.
abstract: Darier disease (DD) is a rare genodermatosis caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene, leading to impaired intracellular calcium signaling, acantholysis, and dyskeratosis. Although traditionally viewed primarily as a cutaneous disorder, DD shows significant intragenerational and intergenerational phenotypic variability and systemic associations. We present an extraordinary case series of 3 patients from a single Turkish family representing 3 successive generations of DD, each demonstrating distinct clinical manifestations alongside varying neuropsychiatric comorbidities. Specifically, the first-generation patient presented with Alzheimer disease, the second with obsessive-compulsive disorder, and the third with cognitive impairment. The diagnosis was supported by classical clinical and histopathological findings. To our knowledge, this is the first report specifically characterizing the spectrum of neuropsychiatric manifestations across 3 consecutive generations within a single family affected by DD. This familial presentation highlights the disease's complex pleiotropic effects and underscores the need for a multidisciplinary approach to evaluating these patients.

title: A novel de novo variant of CDKL5 in an Iranian child with infantile-onset refractory epilepsy.
abstract:
Epilepsy is defined as a long-term brain disease with recurrent and spontaneous seizures that often begin in childhood and encompass a wide range of etiologies, including genetic factors. This study aimed to identify and characterize the genetic cause underlying developmental delay and refractory epilepsy in an Iranian patient.
We performed a prospective evaluation of an Iranian girl presenting with developmental delay, refractory seizures, and hypotonia. The case was referred to the Genetic Research Center, Meybod,, Iran. Whole exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing were performed to identify the disease-causing variant and validate it, respectively. Also, bioinformatic analyses were used to evaluate the predicted pathogenicity and structural consequences of the variants.
A novel de novo frameshift variant in CDKL5 gene (c.1037_1038delTCinsCAGATCTAA, p.Ile346Thrfs*14) was identified and classified as pathogenic based on ACMG criteria. The variant is predicted to engender a premature stop codon, leading to extensive shortening of the protein and loss of essential functional domains. Additionally, Valproate-Lamotrigine combination therapy resulted in significant clinical effects, such as a considerable reduction in the number of seizures.
The present study can expand the mutational spectrum of CDKL5 and highlight the clinical advantage of sequencing-based genetic testing for early diagnosis and personalized therapeutic management of refractory epilepsy.

title: Evaluation of anti-depressant, anxiolytic, and cognitive improvement effects of nanocurcumin using social isolation model in male mice: Behavioral and histopathological evaluation.
abstract: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a heterogeneous mental illness that affects about 10% of people worldwide. Curcumin (Cur) is suggested as a treatment or adjunct treatment of MDD by multiple mechanisms of action. Its effectiveness is limited due to low solubility, poor bioavailability, and rapid metabolization. Different nano-formulations of Cur have been developed to boost its biological activity. The aim of this study was the evaluation of antidepressant/anxiolytic-like effects, and cognitive improvement of nanocurcumin (NCur) in male mice by post-weaning social isolation (PWSI) model to induce depressive/anxiety-like behaviors and cognitive deficits. Mice were housed either in a social group (SG) or an isolated group (IG) for four weeks. After two weeks, IG mice were treated intraperitoneally with NCur (5, 10, 20 mg/kg) and Cur (20 mg/kg) for two weeks. A battery of behavioral tests was used to evaluate depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment. NCur (20 mg/kg) showed antidepressant-like effect in forced swimming test (P < 0.001) and tail suspension test (P < 0.05), anxiolytic-like effect in elevated plus maze (P < 0.05) and open filed test (P < 0.01), and improved the memory and cognition in passive avoidance test (P < 0.05), but Cur (20 mg/kg) had no effect. Histopathology results showed that NCur (5 mg/kg) led to optimal neuronal survival in CA1, improved cellular organization in CA3, and the highest count of normal neurons in the dentate gyrus. NCur demonstrated potential to treat the depressive/anxiety-like behaviors and impaired cognition induced by the PWSI model in male mice. Histopathological data also showed improvements in hippocampal regions.

title: Gray matter volume alterations in generalized anxiety disorder and major depressive disorder.
abstract:
Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and major depressive disorder (MDD) are highly comorbid and clinically overlapping, but their shared and differential structural brain alterations remain unclear. This study investigated gray matter volume (GMV) alterations in GAD and MDD using voxel-based morphometry (VBM).
A total of 168 right-handed participants, including 42 patients with GAD, 43 patients with MDD, and 83 healthy controls (HCs), underwent high-resolution T1-weighted MRI. Whole-brain VBM analyses were performed to compare GMV differences among the three groups, controlling for age, sex, education, and total intracranial volume. Post hoc analyses were conducted for significant clusters, and partial correlation analyses examined associations between abnormal GMV and symptom severity.
Significant group differences in GMV were found in the left middle frontal gyrus, left postcentral gyrus, left putamen, and right superior frontal gyrus. Both GAD and MDD patients showed decreased GMV in the left middle frontal gyrus and left postcentral gyrus, and increased GMV in the left putamen, compared with HCs. In contrast, decreased GMV in the right superior frontal gyrus was observed only in MDD patients and was positively correlated with both anxiety and depressive symptom severity.
These findings suggest that GAD and MDD share GMV alterations in prefrontal, somatosensory, and striatal regions, whereas reduced GMV in the right superior frontal gyrus was observed only in the MDD group.
